articles.title: What a British think tank gets wrong about Russia’s ultimate weapons
articles.body:
What a British think tank gets wrong about Russia’s ultimate weapons
A few days ago, the Royal United Services Institute (RUSI) released a report titled ‘Russia’s Nuclear Deterrent and Its Weapons Procurement’. The report examines the development of Russia’s nuclear triad amid stringent financial constraints and the rising threat of a potential US non-nuclear counterforce strike.
The author of the report, Sidharth Kaushal, makes conclusions based on the publications of Russian military experts in the journal ‘Voennaya Mysl’ (Military Thought), as well as established Western practices for analyzing Russia’s nuclear capabilities.
A British diagnosis of Russia’s nuclear future
Here are the key takeaways from the report:
- Paradigm shift: Russia is being compelled to shift its focus from a posture of “assured retaliation” (increasing the survivability of mobile missile systems and submarine-launched ballistic forces to effectively counter a first strike) to a Launch on Warning (LOW) posture (employing its arsenal early against an enemy attack).
- Vulnerability of mobile forces: Advancements in US space reconnaissance make the concealment of mobile ground-based systems increasingly ineffective.
- Greater reliance on silo-based launchers, which are viewed as more secure bases for strategic missiles. Silo-based systems will comprise a greater proportion of throw weight, particularly since RS-28 Sarmat heavy intercontinental ballistic missiles are silo-launched to ensure instant readiness.
- Economic challenges: According to the report, modern Russia cannot pursue a large-scale quantitative increase in its missile arsenal due to the enormous costs associated with developing and maintaining the conventional armed forces amidst the ongoing military operation in Ukraine.
- Due to cost parity, the domestic production costs of strategic missile systems compete with conventional weaponry – for example, producing one Yars missile is equivalent to the cost of 15 T-72 tanks.
- A labor shortage in the nuclear and missile industries is unavoidable in the current conditions and necessitates a significant increase in wages.
The author also provides interesting assessments of specific weapons systems:
- RS-28 Sarmat: The report projects no quantitative increase in the deployment of these missiles. Emphasis is placed on a short boost phase and a high payload capacity for overcoming missile defense systems.
- The medium-range Oreshnik missile is seen as a priority in the European theater of operations and as a tool for preemptively neutralizing US Dark Eagle systems in Europe. Given manufacturing shortages, it is expected to be deployed primarily in its nuclear variant.
- The long-range KH-BD air-launched cruise missile (with a range up to 6,500 km) is designed to be carried by Tu-95 and Tu-160 bombers, in light of the lack of progress on the PAK DA next-generation stealth strategic bomber.
- Burevestnik and Poseidon programs are considered technically unfeasible by the author of the report; due to the high costs, they are perceived primarily as methods of psychological intimidation
- Space-based warfare: The report highlights the jamming of US missile defense systems as a major priority for Russia. It predicts the launch of nuclear electronic warfare satellites into orbit and the eventual deployment of full-scale space-based nuclear weapons to create massive plasma fields in the ionosphere.
How can we assess this report? Generally, the picture is more complex than described. Like in the Indian parable about the blind men and the elephant, the author of the report sees certain aspects of the ‘elephant’ but fails to see the general picture, which may be quite different. Let’s take a closer look.
The logic behind Russia’s nuclear shield
Regarding the structure of the strategic nuclear forces and the shifting balance between mobile and stationary systems, the distinctive feature of the Soviet, and now Russian, approach lies in balancing mobile and stationary strategic missile systems. Despite advances in satellite reconnaissance, mobile missile systems hold certain advantages: for example, hundreds of them are deployed over vast territories. Moreover, several Peresvet laser weapon systems have already been deployed; these can blind potential adversaries’ optical reconnaissance systems at a critical moment. While reliance on space-based systems is understandable, it’s important to note that these technologies are also vulnerable to various factors, as we have seen recently.
Stationary missile systems come with a significant drawback: it’s relatively easy to spot their location. However, they offer a high level of protection against non-nuclear strikes and maintain relatively high (though not absolute) survivability in the event of a nuclear exchange. Russia’s strategy combines hard-to-detect mobile missile systems with stationary systems that can be employed in response to a nuclear attack. This combination allows for greater flexibility and multiple operational scenarios. Considering this strategy, it’s likely that a large inventory of Sarmat missiles isn’t necessary – two regiments with 50+ missile silos might suffice. This doesn’t indicate a shift in priorities but rather reaffirms a conservative and justified traditional approach.
We must also note the naval component, which ensures reliable retaliatory capability. Both Russian and Western analysts have grown accustomed to the fact that the Bulava submarine-launched solid-fuel missile has been deployed and will eventually replace other ballistic missiles in the Russian Navy. However, that’s not entirely true. Project 667BDRM DELTA-IV submarines equipped with liquid-fueled R-29RM missiles remain on duty. These missiles are among the most effective strategic systems in terms of their energy-mass efficiency. Judging by statements from 2022, it seems that Russia may very well renew its interest in liquid-fueled sea-based missiles. Maintaining two centers for naval missile production is more expensive than having just one, but if it results in a higher number of warheads with fewer missiles, financial concerns could be overlooked.
Lastly, the demonization of the Oreshnik missile in the West is understandable and, overall, justified. Its minimal flight time presents a significant threat. There’s also the option for hybrid use – deploying it with non-nuclear payloads to signal intentions or for use in low-intensity conflicts. The existence of such a missile system increases the range of potential scenarios for employing strategic forces and provides substantial flexibility.
Even a few launch facilities would suffice for these purposes, which raises questions about the costly deployment of multiple brigades. Most likely, we’re talking about the deployment of divisions with 3-4 TELs instead of full brigades consisting of 12 TELs. This strategy also allows to increase the number of deployed missiles, should the need arise.
Beyond the bluff: Weapons built for retaliation
The assessment of the aviation component of the strategic nuclear forces seems fairly accurate, but it’s necessary to note that several other weapon programs are also being developed alongside the KH-BD missiles. Russian defense contractors consistently work on multiple projects, regardless of the current financial climate. It’s reasonable to assume they’re developing air-launched hypersonic missile systems for both tactical and strategic aviation, as well as various types of cruise missiles for strategic use. Additionally, it’s highly likely that a range of tactical munitions for front-line aviation is also under development. Similarly, work on the new PAK DA strategic bomber is probably ongoing, even if the urgent need for this expensive project has diminished.
I’d like to highlight the assessments regarding the Burevestnik nuclear-powered cruise missile and the Poseidon nuclear-powered UUV. Both systems boast practically unlimited range and the ability to remain airborne/underwater for extended periods of time. There’s a lot of speculation and publicity surrounding these projects, and it makes sense to leverage such groundbreaking initiatives for propaganda purposes. However, this doesn’t negate their real military significance or the seriousness of intentions regarding their deployment.
Infrastructure for these projects wouldn’t be carried out solely for PR purposes. At least one major base with several launch systems is being constructed for Burevestnik missiles, and for the Poseidon UUV, basing facilities are being built in the Pacific Ocean, and it is set to be deployed to the Northern Fleet.
Experts monitor progress and construction through satellite imagery. Tracking testing activities is more complex, but there are signs that work continues in this direction as well. Most importantly, these combat systems possess an unknown yet potentially immense retaliatory capability, which is difficult to evaluate due to the absence of analogues. What’s certain is that their potential is significant. Poseidon UUVs may not be able to target naval fleets, but their true purpose is to ensure guaranteed retaliatory strikes capable of causing total destruction along an adversary’s coastline.
In summary, despite economic and financial challenges, Russia will undoubtedly find the resources necessary to maintain and advance its nuclear triad, or even the more powerful new strategic nuclear forces.

articles.title: Ukraine's Neptune Missiles Destroy 2 Russian Su-34 Bombers in Volgograd Region
articles.body:
Ukraine’s Neptunes successfully destroyed two Russian Su-34 fighter-bombers, used by Moscow to launch unguided and guided aerial bombs (KABs), in Russia’s Volgograd region on Thursday, Oct. 29.
The Ukrainian Navy’s Neptune coastal missile system hit the aircraft, which can also carry missiles of various types, at the Marinovka airfield, near the settlement of Oktyabrsky. This was initially reported by the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine (AFU).
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Several minutes later, President Volodymyr Zelensky confirmed the report, noting that Ukraine had carried out two missile strikes during the day. In one of the strikes, a launcher for Russia’s Iskander ballistic missiles was hit as well.
The Su-34, a two-seat long-range strike derivative of the Su-27 fighter, was originally developed in the 1990s, but was only brought into service in 2014.
It is described as Russia’s main aircraft launching KABs on Ukrainian cities nationwide, capable of carrying up to 8 tons of munitions, with an estimated value of each jet at about $50 million.
Such bombs remain one of Russia’s most destructive weapons against Ukrainian cities near the front line. Earlier on Thursday, three KABs struck an apartment building in Izium, Kharkiv region, injuring at least 13 people.
Throughout the day, at least 20 people were killed and 109 wounded in Russian attacks on Ukraine nationwide, with several types of weapons used, including ballistic missiles and first-person-view (FPV) drones.
Putin Says Nordic Leaders Were Right to Call Him, Despite EU Criticism
Second strike on Su-34 in two weeks
The Marinovka airfield, located about 400 kilometers (249 miles) from Ukraine, has previously been targeted by Ukrainian Defense Forces in 2025 as well, as it hosts a squadron of Su-34s.
Overnight Oct. 14-15, Ukraine struck six Russian Su-34 bombers with a Neptune missile strike, at another military airfield in Russia’s Voronezh region. The attack targeted Borisoglebsk airfield and also destroyed equipment used to support flight operations
Originally designed to destroy warships, Neptune is a domestically developed Ukrainian Cruise missile. In April 2022, its ground-based system sank Russia’s shadow fleet vessel, the Moskva.
Since then, Ukraine has upgraded the missile for strikes on land targets deep inside Russia, with the new version capable of reaching targets up to 1,000 kilometers (621 miles) away.
Zelensky warns of fresh ballistic attacks
During the same remarks, Zelensky said Ukraine had obtained intelligence that Russia was preparing fresh ballistic missiles.
He called on partners to provide interceptor packages for Patriot air-defense systems, of which Ukraine is facing a critical shortage. “We are waiting for the relevant decisions,” Zelensky said.
The appeal follows similar warnings during his visit to the Netherlands on Wednesday, Oct. 28, where he described Patriot missiles as Ukraine’s most critical shortage, urging Washington not to delay deliveries under the Prioritized Ukraine Requirements List (PURL) – a mechanism through which allies fund purchases of US-made weapons for Ukraine.
Ahead of winter, Russia is increasingly relying on ballistic missiles to target Ukraine’s critical infrastructure, including the power grid and water supplies.
Meanwhile, Kyiv has reportedly depleted its stocks of Patriot interceptors as early as Oct. 15, due to limited deliveries from allies.
For Ukraine the PAC-3 is among the very few weapons capable of deterring Russia’s ballistic missiles. Russian Iskander-M, for example, is a ballistic missile carrying a half-ton warhead that is strong enough to tear down a quarter to half of a typical apartment block.
“Another aspect of our anti-ballistic work is the interceptor packages, primarily for Patriots, that partners can provide to us,” Zelensky said on Wednesday.

articles.title: North Korea tests attack drones as Kim calls for 'absolute superiority'
articles.body:
North Korea tests attack drones as Kim calls for 'absolute superiority'
North Korea has tested attack drones, cruise missiles and rocket launchers at a weapons demonstration, state media reported Friday, as Kim Jong Un called for faster development of military drone and artificial intelligence technology. The tests follow a series of weapons trials and rising tensions with South Korea.
North Korea has test-fired attack drones, missiles and a multiple rocket launcher at a weapons demonstration, state media reported Friday, as leader Kim Jong Un called for faster development of drone and AI technology for military use.
The event came a day after Seoul said Pyongyang had fired 'around a dozen' short-range ballistic missiles off its east coast, though it was not immediately clear whether the launches were linked to the demonstration.
At the event, Kim stressed the "aim to seize the absolute superiority in the drone technology is an indispensable option in the light of the ever-changing patterns of modern warfare", according to KCNA.
He added: "Strength precisely means peace and peace is guaranteed only by strength."
The demonstration featured suicide attack drones, multipurpose drones firing air-to-surface missiles, cruise missiles and 600mm multiple rocket launchers. KCNA said the drones and cruise missiles hit an island target with 100 per cent accuracy.
The event follows a slew of recent weapons tests by Pyongyang, including a new precision-guided torpedo system and an intermediate-range hypersonic missile, both of which were said to employ AI technology.
Read moreNorth Korea fires 'around a dozen' ballistic missiles amid rising tensions with South Korea
South Korea's Joint Chiefs of Staff said its military detected "around a dozen short-range ballistic missiles fired from the Wonsan area of North Korea towards the East Sea", also known as the Sea of Japan.
The missiles flew about 250 kilometres (155 miles), and "South Korea and the United States are conducting a detailed analysis of their exact specifications", Seoul's military said, adding it had stepped up surveillance of possible additional launches.
Seoul's National Security Office, meanwhile, said the launches violated UN Security Council resolutions, labelling them "serious acts that do nothing to help manage the current situation".
Thursday's missile flurry comes against the backdrop of growing tensions over a landmine explosion along the heavily fortified border between the two Koreas that saw three South Korean soldiers wounded.
A joint Seoul-UN investigation earlier this month concluded that North Korea planted the landmines over a year ago.
Seoul accused Pyongyang of "a clear violation of the Armistice Agreement" and demanded an apology, something the North has mockingly dismissed.
Read moreNorth Korea test-fires submarine-launched cruise missiles amid rising tensions
'Show of force'
Last week, Kim Yo Jong, the powerful sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, said the North would place loudspeakers on standby along the border "within days" and had put unspecified "new counter means" on alert.
Both countries have occasionally turned to loudspeakers blaring propaganda across their shared border and other psychological warfare methods.
South Korea days later proposed military talks with the North to "mutually confirm the precise location" of their border and discuss restoring communication channels, but Pyongyang has yet to respond.
The DMZ is one of the world's most heavily fortified frontiers, and landmine incidents have previously heightened tensions.
Seoul and Pyongyang remain technically at war, as the Korean conflict ended in 1953 with a truce rather than a peace treaty.
The ratcheting tensions come as US President Donald Trump's recent overtures to North Korea have raised concerns that Seoul – an ally of Washington – could be sidelined in potential nuclear talks involving Pyongyang.
In his most recent comments, Trump seemingly downplayed the possibility of a summit while insisting his relationship with Kim Jong Un was "very good".
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

articles.title: When Will US Transfer Operational Control to South Korea? Debate Rages
articles.body:
For years, U.S. and South Korean officials have said they want to reach an arrangement where, should war break out on the peninsula, Seoul’s military commanders would have operational control of American forces there.
Such a setup would be unprecedented in modern times, and what it would mean for U.S. Airmen, Guardians, and other troops remains to be seen. But recent comments from U.S. and Korean leaders underscore just how complex and even controversial the idea remains.
Since World War II, the U.S. has been the ultimate authority for all its combined forces’ wartime operations. But South Korea—officially called the Republic of Korea—has been pressing to finalize the transfer of wartime operational control, or OPCON. Since taking office last year, President Lee Jae Myung has publicly stated his goal is to reach OPCON before his term ends in 2030, and likely earlier.
But the commander of U.S. Forces Korea, Army Gen. Xavier T. Brunson, sounded far more cautious at a Center for Strategic and International Studies summit on Oct. 14. Evolving security concerns, such as recent ballistic missile launches, have created “new standards” that must be met before OPCON can be transferred, Brunson said.
Brunson said the transfer must be “conditions-based” and not follow a political timeline.
His comments spurred immediate backlash from Korean officials, including Defense Minister Kan Shin-chul and National Security Advisor Wi Sung-lac, who claim that Brunson’s remarks about new conditions amount to shifting the goalposts and will make the planned transfer impossible.
On Oct. 29, Sung-lac said during a parliamentary audit that the government had been consulting with Washington to complete the transfer by or before 2030. But a planned Security Consultative Meeting scheduled for December in Washington to discuss various alliance and security concerns has been postponed to next year.
A U.S. Pacific Command spokesperson declined to respond to specific questions regarding the conditions required for transfer but did provide a statement to Air & Space Forces Magazine.
“The transition of wartime operational control (OPCON) remains a conditions-based process mutually agreed upon by the United States and the Republic of Korea,” Navy Lt. Cmdr. Chloe Morgan wrote. “Both nations remain committed to ensuring that the necessary conditions are met before any transition occurs. We will not prejudge decisions or outcomes of this bilateral process.”
While the OPCON process continues and Korean leaders push to move forward, not all American experts agree that it’s a good idea. During an Oct. 27 symposium hosted by the Institute for Korean-American Studies, former USFK commanders Walter Sharp and Paul LaCamera, both Army four-stars, critiqued the weakening of the U.S.-Korea alliance, the Korea JoongAng Daily reported.
“That whole combined nature goes away and … [I] really do see it as a doorway to greatly reducing the alliance, greatly reducing our work with Korea,” Sharp said.
LaCamera was even more pointed.
“It will be suboptimal when the fighting starts, and then we will quickly get to optimization because it is adapt or perish,” he said.
As the debate continues, South Korea is leading combined missions during a two-week, biannual, air-focused Freedom Flag exercise.
The top ROK air commander, Col. Lee Seung-hwan, emphasized his airmen’s role and its ultimate goal.
“While using this as an opportunity to build teamwork among South Korean and U.S. pilots and polish combat skills, we will also cultivate capabilities in preparation for the OPCON transfer,” Seung-hwan said.
To Transfer or Not
The idea behind transferring OPCON to South Korea dates back to the 1980s when President Roh Tae-woo made it a campaign promise in 1987, driven by a desire to strengthen South Korean sovereignty. The United States didn’t transfer peacetime control to Seoul until 1994. Wartime control was expected to soon follow but was derailed during the 1993-1994 North Korean nuclear crisis.
The South Korean push renewed under President Roh Moo-hyun in 2003. Then-U.S. Secretary of Defense Donald Rumsfeld championed the idea, calling it “pushing on an open door” to free up U.S. forces on the peninsula and give the Pentagon more strategic flexibility.
The pair formalized an agreement in 2006 to begin the wartime OPCON transfer.
But getting to the point where the transfer makes sense for both sides isn’t so simple, multiple retired commanders with deep experience on the peninsula told Air & Space Forces Magazine.
“Conditions should determine the timeline,” retired U.S. Army Special Forces Col. David S. Maxwell told Air & Space Forces Magazine. “The timeline should never determine the conditions.”
Maxwell explained that target dates help drive budgets, procurement, training, and accountability, but can’t substitute for demonstrated combat capability.
“If political leaders want to accelerate transition, they must accelerate the fielding of equipment, development of personnel, and combined exercises required to meet the agreed conditions,” Maxwell said. “Political authority cannot manufacture readiness.”
Retired Lt. Gen. David Deptula, Dean of the Mitchell Institute for Aerospace Studies, also emphasized the importance of not rushing the transfer.
“My principal concern would be any arrangement that sacrifices combat effectiveness to satisfy an arbitrary political timeline or the symbolism of transferring command,” Deptula said. “We cannot afford to discover deficiencies in command and control after a conflict begins.”
Still, Maxwell, now vice president of the Center for Asia Pacific Strategy, said changing conditions “cannot become an unexplained justification for indefinite delay.”
“Both allies must identify what has changed, which operational requirements it affects, and what capabilities will close the resulting gaps. We should distinguish the agreed conditions from the evolving military capabilities required to satisfy them,” Maxwell said. “The objective is a successful transition that strengthens deterrence and combined defense. Most importantly, political leaders cannot base decisions on threat assessments from five, 10, or 20 years ago.”
Maxwell and Deptula highlight several critical conditions before OPCON transfer should go through:
- South Korea should demonstrate the capability to lead a combined defense and coordinate offensive actions at scale.
- There should be comprehensive alliance capabilities to respond to North Korean nuclear and missile threats.
- A stable security environment
- Integrated architecture for intelligence, surveillance, reconnaissance, and early warning for near-real-time actionable data
- Integrated air and missile defenses across U.S. and ROK forces
- Secure, resilient command and control in the face of cyber and electronic attacks.
- Sufficient munitions, logistics, infrastructure protection, and sustainment capabilities.
- Certified initial operational capability, full operational capability, and full mission capability assessment results for readiness.
While wartime control of the entire combined U.S.-ROK force is in question, more complex considerations apply to the use of the 7th Air Force, USFK’s air component based at Kunsan and Osan Air Bases in South Korea.
The Air Side
If conflict were to break out today, U.S. and ROK forces would be controlled by a Combined Forces Command that has existed since 1978. The commander of U.S. Forces Korea is dual-hatted as the head of the CFC and has a Korean deputy.
Once the OPCON transfer occurs, that arrangement would flip: a South Korean four-star commander with a U.S. four-star deputy. But even with that combined arrangement, the Pentagon doesn’t cede control of its forces entirely, and it does not give the Korean commander authority over U.S. aircraft in the Pacific.
Retired Lt. Gen. Jeffrey A. Remington, who commanded the 7th Air Force from 2008 to 2012, explained that under the new arrangement, the 7th Air Force commander would still oversee the air component for the Korean general in charge, informing the general on the status of air forces, personnel, and wartime options.
“[The 7th Air Force commander] would continue to be the air component commander, not a Korean, … a U.S. Air Force three-star general,” Remington said.
The commander would then come to the Korean four-star and say, ““Here’s the options, here’s what I can do for you. Here’s the implications of those options,’ and we’ll come to an agreement,” he said.
Even in that arrangement, Remington said Washington likely wouldn’t be involved directly in any major decision involving U.S. forces, especially major airpower assets.
Deptula stressed that in hammering out the details of this arrangement, “the issue is not whether a South Korean general is capable of commanding American airpower. It’s whether the command structure provides the authority, experience, capabilities, and operational flexibility necessary to employ airpower effectively.”
The ROK military is highly professional and capable and a solid U.S. ally in the region, Deptula added. But such a transfer requires more.
“Commanding a modern, integrated air campaign involving hundreds of aircraft, sophisticated intelligence and surveillance capabilities, electronic warfare, space-based systems, and long-range strike assets requires far more than flying airplanes or managing individual missions,” Deptula said.
Day-to-day operations running an Air Operations Center and delivering air tasking orders already happen in a combined way through the AOC at Osan Air Base, Deptula said.
“The real issue is creating a master air attack plan,” he said. “That is the mechanism through which an air campaign translates strategic and operational objectives into coordinated tactical actions. It integrates offensive counterair, defensive counterair, strategic attack, interdiction, close air support, intelligence collection, electronic warfare, air refueling, and other capabilities into a coherent campaign.”
While the U.S. has participated in combined forces operations in World War II and with NATO in Bosnia and Herzegovina and Kosovo, it has never been in a combined force operation without being the ultimate authority for wartime OPCON.
Most U.S. operations during the Global War on Terror and since have been in coalitions. Those typically operate with separate militaries covering different areas, such as the British contribution to the invasion of and early stages of the Iraq War, where their forces were concentrated near Basra and controlled the southeastern section of the war effort near Kuwait.
Combined warfare is different.
“Combined warfare means you’re there together. You’re executing together. You’re mixed and making things happen,” Remington said. “Whereas in a coalition it’s not all that combined, especially from a command-and-control perspective.”
In a very technical sense, for U.S. aviators that might mean being controlled through another nation’s airborne early warning or air battle management systems.
That has been somewhat common with NATO combined forces arrangements in past operations and exercises and with South Korea via their ROKAF Master Control and Reporting Centers. Those two MCRCs serve as nerve centers for all air ops on the peninsula and have operated since the mid-1980s, preceded by a Tactical Air Control Center that ran from the early 1980s until the advent of MCRC.
One MCRC, call sign Watchman, is at Osan. The other, call sign Acacia, is at Daegu Air Base and serves as a reserve aerospace operations center.
Beyond the Peninsula
While 7th Air Force is the USFK air component with primary duties to defend South Korea, it also relies on Pacific Air Forces for support and contributes to PACAF’s needs to support U.S. Pacific Command. U.S. Forces Korea are not on a proverbial island, focused solely on local security concerns.
Should a conflict with China or other regional problems erupt, USAF may need to draw upon 7th Air Force.
“The U.S. military is operating with declining force structure and must meet growing global requirements,” Deptula said. “Aircraft, aircrews, munitions, tankers, intelligence platforms, and other assets cannot be committed to two different campaigns simultaneously without accepting significant operational risk.”
That fact means that contingency planning, force allocation, and command relationships take on even more significance when looking to transfer operational control, Deptula said
“Both nations must understand in advance what capabilities are committed, what reinforcements may be available, and under what circumstances U.S. forces might be required elsewhere,” he said.
Any such transfer “must preserve” U.S. commanders’ ability to employ their capabilities where they can achieve the greatest strategic effect, he said.
“Any future defense of South Korea must begin with an appreciation for the fact that air superiority provides the freedom to attack and the freedom from attack,” Deptula said. “It enables all other military operations. The campaign must be designed to achieve the degree of air superiority necessary to permit the joint force to operate effectively, rather than simply contest the airspace.”

articles.title: Ukraine war latest: 'Russia's mass murder' — Deadly Russian strikes on Dnipro, Chernihiv, Kremenchuk
articles.body:
Ukraine war latest: 'Russia's mass murder' — Deadly Russian strikes on Dnipro, Chernihiv, Kremenchuk
Key developments on Oct. 28:
- 'Russia's mass murder:' Drone strike on Dnipro station kills 14 amid deadly daytime attacks on Chernihiv, Kremenchuk
- Ukraine destroys 2 Russian Su-34 bomber jets in Neptune missile strike on airfield, Navy says
- Route demining completed in Russian-occupied Oleshky as humanitarian convoy prepares to enter, Ukraine's ombudsman says
- Ukraine strikes Russian 'drone port' in Bryansk Oblast, damaging storage facilities, military says
- UN appoints Russian diplomat to oversee mine action, as Ukraine clears over 300,000 explosives in Kherson Oblast
- Russian general charged in absentia for missile strike on museum dedicated to 18th century Ukrainian philosopher
Russian forces struck a train platform at Dnipro railway station on the morning of Oct. 29, killing at least 14 people and wounding at least 14 more, authorities said.
A passenger train was preparing to depart the platform for Zaporizhzhia when the station was attacked by a Russian jet-powered drone, Ukrainian Railways wrote on social media.
The brazen daytime attack was followed in close succession by deadly strikes against civilians in Chernihiv and Kremenchuk.
The strikes on civilians come not only in the middle of a scheduled local ceasefire in Kherson Oblast, agreed to by Kyiv and Moscow to help evacuate and deliver aid to the residents of the occupied city of Oleshky, but also ahead of the first trilateral "peace negotiations" mediated by the United States since February this year.
According to Ukraine's Air Force, Dnipro was attacked around 11:00 a.m. by four Russian jet-powered drones, three of which were downed by Ukrainian air defense before reaching their targets.
Despite the air raid alert and announcements of a heightened threat, people remained on the platform, Ukrainian Railways said.
Passengers were told to evacuate from the stationary train around ten minutes before the strike, with station and train staff checking each train car one by one.
At 11:29 a.m., Dnipropetrovsk Oblast governor Oleksandr Hanzha reported that medics were already at the scene of the attack, providing first aid.
"A horrific Russian attack on Dnipro train station," President Volodymyr Zelensky wrote on social media in response to the attack. "The Russians used a drone to attack a platform where a regular commuter train and a regular passenger train were standing."
"How many such terrorist attacks has Russia carried out on our people after lifting sanctions on some Russian oligarchs and energy companies instead of de-escalating."
Latvian Foreign Minister Baiba Braze described the attack on Dnipro as "mass murder."
Following the Russian attack on Dnipro, 25,000 people in the city and surrounding Oblast were left without electricity, Hanzha said in the afternoon.
Later in the day, Dnipro Mayor Borys Filatov reported that a Russian drone struck the dormitory of a vocational school in Dnipro, setting the entire fifth floor on fire. There were no injuries, Filatov said, as the students had managed to reach the shelter before the strike.
Throughout the day, Russian attacks across Dnipropetrovsk Oblast injured four more people, including a 15-year-old girl, Hanzha said in an evening statement.
Elsewhere across Ukraine, the cities of Chernihiv and Kremenchuk were also targeted by daytime Russian attacks.
Around noon, Russian forces struck the center of Chernihiv in northern Ukraine with Banderol cruise missiles, killing two 15-year-old girls, regional governor Viacheslav Chaus said.
At least 25 more people were injured in the attack, including four children, the youngest one 10-months-old, Chaus later said.
Meanwhile, in the city of Kremenchuk in Poltava Oblast, at least three people were killed and 32 injured, including six children and two people still in critical condition, after Russian drones struck an apartment building in a residential area, according to local authorities. Oct. 30 has been declared a day of mourning in Poltava Oblast.

Ukraine destroys 2 Russian Su-34 bomber jets in Neptune missile strike on airfield, Navy says
Ukraine's Navy destroyed two Russian Su-34 fighter-bomber jets in a strike against the Marinovka military airfield in Russia's Volgograd Oblast, using domestically produced Neptune missiles, the Navy reported on Oct. 29.
The aircraft were destroyed at the base of Russia's 11th Mixed Aviation Regiment near the settlement of Oktyabrsky, according to the Navy. The regiment belongs to the 4th Mixed Aviation Division of Russia's 4th Air and Air Defense Forces Army. The Navy did not provide any visual confirmation of the strike. The Kyiv Independent could not independently verify the claim.
Later on Oct. 29, President Volodymyr Zelensky confirmed the destruction of the two Su-34 jets, adding that Ukrainian forces had also hit a Russian Iskander missile launcher.
The Su-34 is one of Russia's main aircraft used to launch guided aerial bombs against Ukrainian cities, frontline settlements, and military positions. Strikes against these aircraft could weaken Russia's ability to carry out such attacks, while replacing the losses requires significant time and resources.
Russia had approximately 140 Su-34 fighter-bombers of various modifications in service as of Oct. 22, including the modernized Su-34M, Ukraine's military intelligence agency (HUR) reported on Oct. 29.
According to the agency, Russia has lost 43 Su-34 aircraft destroyed and another seven damaged since the start of its full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
"Such losses are quite significant for the aggressor's aircraft fleet, whose restoration requires a lengthy production cycle, substantial financial resources, and specialized industrial cooperation," HUR said.
The agency estimated that Russia can manufacture approximately 14 to 18 Su-34 aircraft annually, meaning the number of destroyed aircraft is equivalent to roughly 2.5–3 years of production.

Route demining completed in Russian-occupied Oleshky as humanitarian convoy prepares to enter, Ukraine's ombudsman says
Demining of designated routes in Russian-occupied Oleshky in Kherson Oblast has been completed, and a humanitarian convoy is ready to depart, Ukraine's Human Rights Commissioner Dmytro Lubinets announced on Oct. 29.
The convoy is expected to arrive at the city's central hospital, where humanitarian assistance will be provided to residents, Lubinets said.
Residents wishing to leave the city will be able to do so until 2:00 p.m. local time, with security measures arranged for their evacuation. Humanitarian aid distribution is scheduled to begin after 2:30 p.m., according to the ombudsman.
Delegations from Ukraine, Russia, and the United States have gathered to coordinate the next steps of the mission, with journalists from all three countries also present, Lubinets said.
The mission is being carried out jointly with Russian Human Rights Commissioner Yana Lantratova, with mediation and coordination by U.S. first lady Melania Trump.
"Our shared goal is to deliver humanitarian aid to civilians and facilitate the safe departure of everyone who wishes to leave the city," Lubinets said.
The operation follows a temporary ceasefire in and around Oleshky, announced by the White House on Oct. 23 and subsequently confirmed by Ukraine and Russia. The pause in fighting, which began on Oct. 27, is expected to remain in effect until Nov. 1 to allow aid deliveries, mine clearance, and civilian evacuations.

Ukraine strikes Russian 'drone port' in Bryansk Oblast, damaging storage facilities, military says
Ukrainian forces have struck a Russian military facility used to launch long-range attack drones at Ukraine, the General Staff said on Oct. 29.
The overnight attack targeted the Russian drone base near Navlya in Bryansk Oblast, around 70 kilometers from the Ukrainian border.
According to the General Staff, the strikes damaged a storage facility for Russian long-range Geran-type drones, as well as fuel and lubricant storage facilities and the 'drone port' itself.
Ukrainian media and open-source intelligence (OSINT) groups have tracked Russia's building of several large 'airfields' designed for unmanned systems and built across Russia's western border areas.
The building of these new 'drone ports' reflects Moscow's growing investment in long-range attack drones as a long-term strategic tool, which can be used both against Ukraine or against countries on NATO's eastern flank.
The Oct. 29 attack was the second strike on the Navlya facility, with the first being on Aug. 3, also targeting launch and storage facilities.
read also
UN appoints Russian diplomat to oversee mine action, as Ukraine clears over 300,000 explosives in Kherson Oblast
The United Nations has appointed a Russian diplomat to a senior position overseeing mine action, drawing criticism from Ukraine as the country continues to clear hundreds of thousands of explosive devices left behind by Russia's war.
U.N. Secretary-General Antonio Guterres announced the appointment of Gleb Desyatnikov as assistant secretary-general for mine action and police in the Department of Peace Operations on Oct. 27.
Desyatnikov has served as Russia's ambassador to Jordan since 2018, including throughout Moscow's full-scale invasion of Ukraine. According to the U.N., he has more than 35 years of experience in international relations and security affairs, including previous positions at Russia's Foreign Ministry.
"Moscow has mined the United Nations," Ukrainian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Heorhii Tykhyi wrote on X on Oct. 29, criticizing the decision.
"Entrusting this responsibility to a representative of the aggressor state is deeply troubling and undermines trust in the United Nations," he added.
The appointment comes as Ukraine faces one of the world's largest demining challenges, with Russian mines and unexploded ordnance threatening civilians and complicating the recovery of agricultural land and infrastructure.
In southern Kherson Oblast, demining teams have neutralized 300,691 explosive devices on the Ukrainian-controlled right bank since the start of clearance operations, according to the regional military administration.
Between Oct. 22 and 28 alone, specialists surveyed 602.8 hectares (1,490 acres) and neutralized 471 explosive devices, the administration reported on Oct. 29. Authorities said 74.5% of the territory designated for clearance on the region's right bank has now been cleared.
read also
Russian general charged in absentia for missile strike on museum dedicated to 18th century Ukrainian philosopher
A Russian lieutenant general has been charged in absentia with ordering the strike on the Kharkiv Oblast museum dedicated to 18th-century philosopher Hryhorii Skovoroda, the Prosecutor General reported on Oct. 29.
On May 6, 2022, a Russian missile struck the museum, located in the village of Skovorodynivka, some 55 kilometers (about 35 miles) from the regional capital. The strike did not completely destroy the museum, but left it in serious disrepair.
According to the Prosecutor General, the Russian lieutenant general who ordered the attack is originally from the village of Chuhuiv in Kharkiv Oblast and commands Russia's 6th Guards Air and Air Defense Forces Army.
"The (lieutenant) general knew for certain that he was attacking not a military target but a monument of Ukrainian culture. Despite this, he gave the combat order to destroy it," the Prosecutor General wrote.
Skovoroda is considered one of the most influential philosophers in Ukrainian intellectual history. His written works are vital contributions to the Ukrainian Baroque and Enlightenment traditions. The building that housed the museum was once the estate where Skovoroda spent his final years and died in 1794.
Russia has repeatedly targeted Ukraine's cultural heritage since the start of the full-scale war. As of September 2026, 2,161 cultural heritage sites and 2,665 cultural institutions in Ukraine had been damaged or destroyed, according to data collected by the Culture Ministry.

articles.title: US military movements don't signal decision to strike: Israel prepares, waits on Trump again
articles.body:
Is the United States preparing to resume its war against Iran? When could another attack take place, and what would its objectives be? A series of military movements observed in recent weeks has raised these questions, but there is still no clear indication that President Donald Trump has decided to order renewed strikes. 
Israel's defense establishment is preparing for the possibility of another conflict, both offensively and defensively, while security officials stress that the developments remain preliminary and are intended, at least in part, to give the president military options should he decide to act.
One of the most significant developments involves the deployment of U.S. forces in the Arabian Sea, near Iran's coast. Twelve American destroyers have been operating in the area in recent weeks, up from approximately eight to 10 previously. Some may be involved in the naval blockade, but the increased presence is also being examined in the context of preparations for a possible military campaign. Two U.S. aircraft carriers are also stationed in the region, while a third is expected to complete its deployment near Japan. Washington will then have to decide whether to send it to the Arabian Sea as reinforcements or use it to replace one of the carriers already there.
Is overthrowing Iran's regime back on the table?
Alongside the naval buildup, preliminary indications of increased American air activity have also emerged. According to an analysis by Israel's Institute for National Security Studies (INSS), aircraft tracking data cautiously suggests that the United States is rebuilding its aerial refueling network in Europe, potentially providing a staging point for moving additional forces into the area covered by U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM). Between Wednesday and Thursday, an American RC-135 reconnaissance aircraft flew from the United States to Britain, while eight C-17 military transport aircraft landed in southern Israel. The assessment is that the aircraft were carrying air defense equipment and logistical supplies, potentially indicating preparations to reinforce defensive systems and offensive capabilities. The IDF has not commented on reports of the landings.
Security officials emphasize that the movements do not necessarily indicate a decision to attack. Trump could still pursue a diplomatic solution, and the scale of the preparations primarily reflects Washington's desire to keep the military option available. "The Americans are preparing options for the president, if and when he decides to launch an attack," a security official said.
The central question is what the objectives of another military campaign would be if one were launched. During Operation Rising Lion, Israel struck Iranian nuclear facilities, with the United States joining the campaign toward its conclusion by attacking the Fordow nuclear facility. During Operation Roaring Lion, which lasted 42 days, nuclear targets were largely avoided. Instead, the campaign focused on weapons manufacturing facilities, military and national infrastructure, Iran's navy and missile systems, alongside more limited strikes against symbols of the regime and the Basij paramilitary forces affiliated with the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.
Another factor is Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's declaration ahead of Israel's elections that he had instructed the country's security agencies to advance a plan to overthrow the Iranian regime in cooperation with Trump. Netanyahu intensified his rhetoric on the issue in the days leading up to the vote and on Election Day itself. The IDF's Military Intelligence Directorate and Israeli Air Force are continuing to update their target lists, divided into categories including infrastructure, nuclear facilities, military buildup and missile capabilities. Any effort to overthrow the Iranian regime would also require a comprehensive operational plan developed by the Mossad intelligence agency in coordination with other Israeli security bodies.
Israeli defense officials are also considering the possibility that Iran could launch an attack of its own, driven by mounting economic distress and fears of another American-Israeli operation after having been caught off guard by major opening strikes on two previous occasions.
"In systems like the American military, preparing the available options takes time," a senior security official explained. "We are talking about weeks, certainly when it comes to a broad military campaign rather than a limited operation, even if it is a short one, as foreign media reports have suggested." The official said it remains difficult to predict Trump's decision. Even if the president authorizes renewed fighting, an attack would not necessarily follow immediately. Israel would prefer a short, intensive campaign, particularly after Operation Roaring Lion stretched to 42 days, considerably longer than initially planned.
Hezbollah prepares for possible confrontation
Military preparations are unfolding alongside diplomatic efforts. According to reports in recent days, U.S. Vice President JD Vance sent a letter to Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council and a figure considered close to Mojtaba Khamenei, to explore the possibility of renewing negotiations between Washington and Tehran. American officials said the initiative was undertaken with Trump's knowledge and at his direction. At the same time, the president continues to threaten a return to military action, potentially after the U.S. midterm elections. The simultaneous diplomatic contacts and military movements leave open the possibility that Washington is seeking to increase pressure on Tehran while preparing for potential military action.
Another concern is Israel's northern front. Israeli defense officials are preparing for the possibility that renewed fighting against Iran could expand into a confrontation with Hezbollah in Lebanon. During the past month, Israeli interceptor missiles have been launched near the Lebanese border. The IDF has not disclosed the targets of those interceptions, but Israeli assessments suggest that at least some may have involved Hezbollah reconnaissance drones attempting to gather intelligence on Israeli troop deployments. Hezbollah has also been moving weapons and preparing for the possibility of renewed fighting with the IDF.
Israel's Northern Command is working to reinforce defensive lines held by Israeli forces in southern Lebanon, establish positions offering greater control through observation and firepower, and prepare plans for capturing additional Hezbollah strongholds.
A renewed conflict could also affect Israel's political situation, with uncertainty continuing over the formation of a governing coalition following the elections. Another war against Iran could reshape the public agenda, alter the balance of power among political parties and place national security and relations with Washington back at the center of political debate. For now, Israel continues updating its military plans while Washington maintains both diplomatic contacts and threats of renewed action. Whether the preparations will lead to another military campaign, and what its objectives might be, remains uncertain.

articles.title: Poland hands Ukraine two more MiG-29 fighter jets
articles.body:
- Poland will soon transfer two MiG-29 fighters to Ukraine in a new aid package worth about €50 million, Rzeczpospolita reported.
- One jet has reached the end of its service life and may be used for spare parts, while the other is still flying.
Poland will soon hand Ukraine two more MiG-29 fighter jets as part of a new military aid package worth about €50 million (about $56 million), Polish daily Rzeczpospolita reported on Oct. 29, in a story quickly picked up by Ukrainian defense outlet Milarnyi.
Reserve Lt. Gen. Dariusz Łukowski, director of the Polish Defense Ministry’s Strategy and Defense Planning Department, confirmed the transfer to the newspaper and said the decision had been made, without giving a date beyond “in the near future.” Only one of the two jets is still flying. The other has reached the end of its service life, and Rzeczpospolita reported that Ukraine may use it as a source of spare parts.
The rest of the package is mostly munitions. Rzeczpospolita reported that Poland will also send 155 mm and 152 mm artillery shells, 20 mm rounds for the six-barrel cannon fitted to F-16 fighters, which Ukrainian pilots use to shoot down Russian drones, and missiles for the Piorun shoulder-fired air defense system built by Polish manufacturer Mesko. Ukrainian defense officials had said in September that the Polish donation would be worth €50 million and would include air defense equipment. Poland’s Defense Ministry declined to detail the contents, saying only that the package draws on equipment being retired by the Polish armed forces or no longer needed.
The two aircraft are a small addition to a fleet Poland has been feeding since the early part of the war. Poland began openly handing over MiG-29s in March 2023, and by that May then-Defense Minister Mariusz Błaszczak said Ukraine had received 10 of them, Militarnyi reported. In total, Poland has given Ukraine 14 MiG-29s, Militarnyi said. Rzeczpospolita reported the same figure, adding that the jets were sent in 2022 and 2023 in varying technical condition and with little publicity.
A further transfer has been discussed for more than two years. In July 2024, Poland’s security agreement with Ukraine included a pledge to consider sending at least one more MiG-29 squadron, but Prime Minister Donald Tusk said Warsaw could not simply give up jets still flying air policing missions unless allies supplied replacements. At the time, the Polish Air Force still had 14 MiG-29s: 11 single-seat MiG-29As and three two-seat MiG-29UB trainers.
In late 2025, the two governments began talks on the last Polish MiG-29s. Defense Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz said the handover would benefit Poland because Warsaw would receive Ukrainian drone and missile technology in return. That exchange has not happened. As of mid-June 2026, Poland’s deputy defense minister said no aircraft from that batch had been delivered, and Rzeczpospolita reported the technology transfer stalled at the political level after Ukraine’s president named a military unit after heroes of the Ukrainian Insurgent Army, a wartime nationalist force whose legacy is deeply contested in Poland.
Poland can spare the jets because their missions are moving to newer aircraft. The MiG-29 has kept a shrinking quick reaction alert role over the Baltic, and Rzeczpospolita reported that its tasks are now handled by Polish F-16s and the first 12 South Korean-built FA-50 light fighters, which reached full operational readiness in 2026.
For Ukraine, every additional airframe matters. The Ukrainian Air Force still relies heavily on the Soviet-designed MiG-29, which it has kept flying through deliveries from Poland, Slovakia and Bulgaria and through cannibalizing retired jets for parts, while losing aircraft to Russian strikes on airfields and in the air.
The new package also follows a separate Polish contribution of Patriot interceptors. Rzeczpospolita reported that Poland has given Ukraine 10 PAC-3 MSE missiles in total, five earlier this year and five more through an international donation led by the United States with NATO. Kosiniak-Kamysz said in July that Poland’s donations to Ukraine since 2022 were worth about 16.45 billion zlotys, most of them delivered in 2022 and 2023, and the ministry later declassified the full list of transferred equipment.

articles.title: North Korea fires 'around a dozen' ballistic missiles amid rising tensions with South Korea
articles.body:
North Korea fires 'around a dozen' ballistic missiles amid rising tensions with South Korea
North Korea fired around a dozen short-range ballistic missiles off its east coast on Thursday, Seoul's defence ministry said. The North Korean capital Pyongyang has stepped up weapons tests in recent weeks despite South Korea's offer of military talks.
North Korea fired "around a dozen" short-range ballistic missiles off its east coast on Thursday, Seoul's defence ministry said, less than a week after South Korea proposed talks over a growing border row.
The launches follow a slew of recent weapons tests by Pyongyang, including a new precision-guided torpedo system and an intermediate-range hypersonic missile, both of which were said to employ AI technology.
Read moreNorth Korea test-fires submarine-launched cruise missiles amid rising tensions
South Korea's Joint Chiefs of Staff (JCS) said its military detected "around a dozen short-range ballistic missiles fired from the Wonsan area of North Korea towards the East Sea" – the body of water also known as the Sea of Japan.
The missiles flew about 250 kilometres, and "South Korea and the United States are conducting a detailed analysis of their exact specifications", Seoul's military said, adding it had stepped up surveillance of possible additional launches.
The Japan Coast Guard had earlier urged ships in the area to be vigilant.
Seoul's National Security Office meanwhile, said the launches violated UN Security Council resolutions, labelling them "serious acts that do nothing to help manage the current situation".
Thursday's missile flurry comes against the backdrop of growing tensions over a landmine explosion along the heavily fortified border between the two Koreas that saw three South Korean soldiers wounded.
A joint Seoul-UN investigation earlier this month concluded that North Korea planted the landmines over a year ago.
Seoul accused the North's capital Pyongyang of "a clear violation of the Armistice Agreement" and demanded an apology, something the North has mockingly dismissed.
'Show of force'
"This should be seen as a fairly high-level show of force," Lim Eul-chul, a professor at South Korea's Kyungnam University, told AFP.
"North Korea is demonstrating that it has the capability to completely destroy major South Korean and US military facilities," he said.
Pyongyang was also sending a political message, Lim added, by "showing off its overwhelming military power and warning Seoul not to interfere with its efforts to fortify the border".
Last week, Kim Yo Jong, the powerful sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong-un, said the North would place loudspeakers on standby along the border "within days" and had put unspecified "new counter means" on alert.
Both countries have occasionally turned to loudspeakers blaring propaganda across their shared border and other psychological warfare methods.
South Korea days later proposed military talks with the North to "mutually confirm the precise location" of their border and discuss restoring communication channels, but Pyongyang is yet to respond.
Read moreNorth Korea launches ballistic missile as tensions with Seoul grow over border mine blasts
The DMZ is one of the world's most heavily fortified frontiers, and landmine incidents have previously heightened tensions between the two countries.
Seoul and Pyongyang remain technically at war, as the Korean conflict ended in 1953 with a truce, rather than a peace treaty.
The ratcheting tensions come as US President Donald Trump's recent overtures to North Korea have raised concerns that Seoul – an ally of Washington – could be sidelined in potential nuclear talks involving Pyongyang.
In his most recent comments, Trump seemingly downplayed the possibility of a summit while insisting his relationship with Kim Jong-Un was "very good".
In October, North Korea launched several short-range ballistic missiles a day after Trump suggested the two might meet this year.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

articles.title: The United States may delay the delivery of Patriot missiles to Ukraine until the elections — media reports
articles.body:
The United States may delay the delivery of Patriot missiles to Ukraine until the elections — media reports
Kyiv • UNN
NATO allies fear that the United States will postpone transferring Patriot missiles to Ukraine until the November 3 midterm elections. Kyiv is awaiting Hegseth’s signature.
The United States may postpone the delivery of Patriot interceptor missiles to Ukraine until the midterm elections, which will be held on November 3. Euronews reports, according to UNN.
Details
According to the publication, Ukraine has appealed to U.S. Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth with a request to sign an agreement on the delivery of key Patriot air defense systems, which are used to intercept Russian ballistic missiles.
However, NATO allies are increasingly pessimistic that Ukraine will receive the urgently needed U.S.-made Patriot interceptor missiles before next week's U.S. midterm elections, amid suspicions that President Donald Trump is using military aid to force Kyiv to make concessions.
The publication's sources note that there is currently no clarity as to whether the United States will provide Patriot missiles to Ukraine.
Trump is using all his leverage over Ukraine ahead of the midterm elections
The source suggested that Trump is also seeking to push Kyiv toward a peace deal involving territorial concessions.
At the same time, two sources said that Washington is frustrated by the lack of progress in ending Russia's war against Ukraine and wants the conflict to end as soon as possible.
One source called the war a "stone in Washington's shoe," but said that the United States understands the need to maintain relations with NATO allies, particularly in the context of the war in Iran.
Recall
Ukraine is working on several fronts - both with the United States and with Europe and other partners - to secure missiles for Patriot systems. In particular, we have been waiting for almost a month for Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth's signature regarding missiles for Patriot and NASAMS systems. Ukrainian officials have been instructed to discuss this with the American side once again.

articles.title: Flash: Russia produces more ballistic missiles than the entire world produces Patriot missiles
articles.body:
Flash: Russia produces more ballistic missiles than the entire world produces Patriot missiles
According to a Ukrinform correspondent, this was stated during a briefing by Serhii “Flash” Beskrestnov, a special advisor to the President.
“Russia produces more ballistic missiles than the world produces ‘Patriots’ to counter them. In other words, this balance looks very strange. If we add North Korean missiles to this, and the missiles produced by Iran, then we realize that global production of anti-ballistic missiles—such as the PAC-3, for example—needs to be increased. But there are currently problems and limitations, and while the Pentagon is trying to increase these production volumes, it’s difficult to do so,” Beskrestnov noted.
He noted that Ukraine could obtain licenses to manufacture anti-ballistic missiles, but the problem lies in the backlog for their components.
To address the shortage of anti-ballistic missiles, Ukraine is requesting that missiles be provided on loan, which it would later return once it begins domestic production; however, due to the unstable global situation, European partners are unwilling to agree to such a move. For its part, the U.S., which has a sufficient supply of PAC-3s, is very limited in how many it is willing to provide.
“These missiles are in the United States, and there’s a stockpile there—some say 3,000, others 4,000; there are 5,000 missiles in the U.S.—and to protect Kyiv, for example, where the ‘Patriot’ system is deployed, through the winter, we need about 4–5% of the U.S. stockpile. That’s a very small portion. And we’re asking the U.S.: ‘Give us this, because the Russians will destroy our infrastructure,’ but this requires a political decision. A decision from the U.S. government. They could give us these missiles—it wouldn’t affect their own defense, because, as I’ve already said, it’s literally 4 percent. But they won’t. We’re receiving a very small number, and we see what’s happening now. I actually believe this is our number one problem,” Beskrestnov noted.
According to the adviser, the situation on the front lines is currently stable, and Ukraine will be able to withstand the enemy even in the event of additional mobilization in Russia. At the same time, the biggest problem today is urban warfare and the enemy’s intention to completely destroy Ukraine’s economic potential.
“Even if they mobilize an additional 300,000 people, that solves nothing. We’ll simply produce more FPVs and field more crews to attack the Russians. We’re already facing the problem that our troops aren’t meeting their targets because there simply aren’t that many Russians to begin with. It sounds very strange, but it’s true. In other words, we understand that the war has changed,” the adviser noted.
According to him, the enemy is destroying infrastructure, bridges, and warehouses in order to cripple Ukraine’s economy.
Beskrestnov emphasized that the enemy is currently stockpiling missiles and “Shahed” drones to continue attacking critical infrastructure. Kyiv will be the primary target, as the capital is a symbolic city for the Russian occupiers.
“Kyiv is a symbolic place for our enemy. They understand that the government is here, and they understand that the international community is watching Kyiv. That is why they want to attack Kyiv specifically,” the adviser emphasized.
As reported by Ukrinform, Ukraine currently needs an aid package consisting of PAC-2 and PAC-3 missiles from Europe and several other countries; subsequently, the FREYJA anti-ballistic missile program will become operational, and contracts with Germany for the procurement of the relevant interceptors will take effect.

articles.title: US deploys 10 military cargo planes to Israel amid preparations for possible strike on Iran: Report
articles.body:
Said Amori and Sahin Demir
30 October 2026•Update: 30 October 2026
The US has transferred 10 military cargo aircraft to Israeli air bases in the southern Negev region amid preparations for a possible military strike against Iran, the Israeli public broadcaster KAN reported Thursday.
The broadcaster said the aircraft landed at Ovda and Nevatim air bases, while additional US military planes were reportedly dispatched to bases in Jordan, Saudi Arabia and Qatar.
According to KAN, the planes departed from Fort Bliss in the US state of Texas, which houses one of the US military’s largest air defense centers, including facilities associated with interceptor missiles and air defense batteries.
There was no immediate US confirmation of the reported deployments, and it remained unclear what cargo the aircraft were carrying or whether Washington had decided to launch an attack against Iran.
An Israeli official told the broadcaster that Israel and the US were closely coordinating their military preparations.
“Israel and the United States are coordinating closely, and although no decision has yet been made on the matter, the Americans and Israel are preparing for any decision President Donald Trump makes,” the official said.
The official did not specify the nature or timing of any potential decision.
Earlier this week, KAN reported that Washington had warned Gulf countries about the possibility of a short, limited military campaign against Iran.
According to the broadcaster, the US military has also transferred a Patriot missile defense system from Texas to reinforce its air defenses in the Gulf region.
The report said US troops stationed at bases across the region had been instructed to leave as a precaution against a possible military escalation.
It added that US forces were replenishing their weapons stockpiles, with an additional aircraft carrier and Marine Corps unit expected to arrive in November.
The reinforcements would reportedly join approximately 20 US warships already operating in the Middle East.
Separately, The Wall Street Journal reported earlier Thursday that US Central Command (CENTCOM) Commander Gen. Brad Cooper had briefed Trump on options for potential strikes against Iran.
The newspaper suggested that the briefing could indicate that Washington was moving closer to launching major military operations.
Democratic US Sen. Chris Murphy said he and several other senators had received a briefing on possible plans to attack Iran, describing them as “insane.”
Murphy warned that such an operation would lead to a devastating escalation and could undermine the US commitment to the rule of law.
The US and Israel launched attacks against Iran on Feb. 28, prompting Tehran to retaliate against Israel and US targets across the region before a ceasefire agreement was reached in April.
The US and Iran signed a memorandum of understanding in June concerning freedom of navigation through the Strait of Hormuz, but its implementation has stalled over disagreements related to the waterway’s security.
The latest reported military deployments come amid renewed concerns over a possible escalation between the US and Iran.

articles.title: Russo-Ukrainian war, day 1709: Russian jet drone kills 14 on Dnipro railway platform beside a Zaporizhzhia-bound train
articles.body:
Exclusives
Military
“The enemy has changed tactics”: Zaporizhzhia faces record number of Russian FPV drone attacks, hitting public transport 3 times in one day. The attacks injured 14 people, including a 14-year-old boy, and damaged residential buildings, warehouses, and vehicles.
Ukrainian Neptune strike destroys two Russian Su-34 bombers used to attack frontline cities, Ukraine’s Navy says. The aircraft are a key part of Russia’s tactical aviation fleet, used to launch guided aerial bombs against Ukrainian military positions and settlements near the front line.
Russia’s October losses hit record high of 49,040 with three days left, Ukraine says. Russia’s estimated personnel losses reached a new monthly high by 29 October, surpassing the previous record set in December 2024.
Russian jet drone hits Dnipro railway platform, killing 14 people next to a Zaporizhzhia-bound train. An air alert was on and the railway had ordered an evacuation, but many passengers were still beside the train when the drone struck.
Baking soda by day, armor chemistry on contract: drones reportedly strike Russia’s Bashkir Soda Company. The plant, which Russian Telegram channel Astra says sits on a closed register of defense suppliers, is the country’s only producer of a chemical used in bulletproof fibers.
Russia may use the Oleshky truce to rebuild its forces, ISW warns, as evacuees face a route through Russia and Belarus. The agreement spells out every leg of the evacuees’ trip except the last one home.
Promised discharge, but no trust: Why Ukraine’s new military contracts are struggling. Only 8,600 Ukrainians have signed the army’s new fixed-term contracts in four months.
Ukraine may already be pushing Operation Vivaldi across the Zherebets River. It’s a risky gamble. Two mappers put Ukrainian troops on the river’s eastern bank this week, including at Terny, where Russia crossed in 2024 and kept pushing until Vivaldi drove it back.
Nearly 5,000 tons of nitric acid for Russia’s military-industrial complex. Why did Azot plant become strategic target?. A military observer explains why Ukraine keeps striking Russia’s Azot plant.
Intelligence and technology
Ukraine finds Russia’s Geran drones fitted with a compass that works through GPS jamming, but Western electronics still at their core. Ukraine is also studying a new jamming device, and the findings go into its sanctions work.
Russian “Susanin” drone component may push Ukraine into nighttime blackouts. Roads and highways would go dark first, presidential adviser says. Ukraine may have to rethink its wartime blackouts if Russia begins mass use of drones and missiles carrying the “Susanin” optical-navigation module.
Russia is building Starlink no foreign company can switch off. Ukraine names 49 firms behind it, and 23 face no sanctions from Kyiv’s allies at all. One of them is Roscosmos, which puts the satellites in orbit.
Licensed, not banned: what China’s new rules mean for the parts inside Russia’s Shahed-type drones. Ukraine’s sanctions commissioner says Geran engines are on Beijing’s updated list and sees an opening for Kyiv.
International
Some European diplomats doubt Seoul over what they see as a tilt toward Russia during Moscow’s war on Ukraine, but Seoul says it backs ending the war, FT reports. Kyiv has already clashed with Seoul over fuel reaching Russia and two North Korean prisoners of war.
Russia’s sanctioned top diplomat heads to the US to campaign against the sanctions on its war. Moscow says Lavrov will use the G20 meeting in Atlanta to denounce sanctions, the economic pressure built to make Russia pay for invading Ukraine.
Germany holds two 19-year-olds over Bulgaria’s Starlink arson, and Sofia says they also attacked the network Ukraine fights with elsewhere in the EU. Bulgaria wants them extradited, and their lawyers say they will fight the warrant.
“I really don’t want this to be Yalta 2, 3, 4”: Zelenskyy fears Trump-Xi-Putin meeting could redivide world, with Ukraine on agenda. Great powers may sit down to redraw the world’s spheres of influence again.
Russia abducts Ukrainian children, and the Netherlands now funds UN search for them as part of new €1.2 billion aid package. Dutch companies get a way into rebuilding Ukraine: €136 million for partnerships and more export insurance in a new aid package.
Humanitarian and social impact
Classrooms in Sumy Oblast are moving underground due to Russian shelling: 13 such schools are already operating, nine are under construction, and another 14 are at the design stage. Russian attacks have damaged 165 schools in Sumy Oblast since the start of the full-scale invasion.
Demining complete, humanitarian convoy ready: Oleshky mission advances as ceasefire holds and Lubinets heads to occupied city. Ukrainian, Russian, and US delegations are coordinating a humanitarian operation in occupied Oleshky after mine clearance along designated routes. The mission aims to bring aid to civilians and facilitate their safe departure.
Six lanes and metro line under fire: Kyiv prepares about $22 million for backup river crossings after Russian strike on Southern Bridge. The bridges are of critical importance. About 600,000 vehicles cross the Dnipro River in Kyiv every day.
Russia may not give Oleshky evacuees a free choice to return to Ukraine, ISW warns, after Putin called the town a “Russian settlement”. Those who choose Ukraine will likely have to travel through Russia first, with no public guarantees that they will be let go.
Political and legal developments
Ankara tells Washington it’s ready to help revive Ukraine-Russia talks—but names no date or venue. Moscow claims a contact is near but that talk of Abu Dhabi is premature while it is still preparing. Kyiv wants that round before a summit without Ukraine.
€100 million at stake: what Ukrainians could save by joining Europe’s euro-payment zone, if parliament votes before November. Ukrainian small businesses pay for every euro transfer in paperwork and days of waiting.
Ukraine wants its Abu Dhabi talks with Russia before a proposed Trump-Putin-Xi summit. Tusk pointed to a first Abu Dhabi round after 4 November. Kyiv says the meeting now depends on Washington.

articles.title: Aid mission set to enter Ukraine's Oleshky as localised ceasefire holds for third day
articles.body:
Aid mission set to enter Ukraine's Oleshky as localised ceasefire holds for third day
A humanitarian aid mission is set to enter the Ukrainian town of Oleshky, a Ukrainian official said on Thuirsday, as a localised truce between Kyiv and Moscow, brokered by US first lady Melania Trump, held for a third day. Some 2,000 residents in the Russian occupied city have been cut off from essential supplies amid reports that many are starving.
Humanitarian aid is poised to roll into the stricken city of Oleshky, a Ukrainian official said Thursday, as a localised ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine stretched into a third day and military units cleared away landmines.
Moscow and Kyiv have observed the truce in and around the devastated southern Ukrainian city since Tuesday, but remain otherwise locked in the war that began with Russia’s full-scale invasion more than 4 ½ years ago. Previous efforts to secure ceasefires either never worked out or the truces quickly fell apart.
Elsewhere, a jet-powered Russian drone hit two passenger trains stopped at a station in Dnipro in central Ukraine on Thursday, killing at least 14 people and injuring 14 more, including a 40-year-old man whose legs were amputated, officials said.
Read moreAt least 13 killed in 'horrific' Russian drone strike at Ukraine train station
Also, a Russian cruise missile killed two 15-year-old girls in the northern city of Chernihiv, and three more civilians died when a Russian drone hit an apartment block in the central Ukraine city of Kremenchuk, authorities said. In all, 56 people were injured in the strikes, including 10 children.
Russia’s Defence Ministry said air defences downed 1,214 Ukrainian drones overnight in one of the largest drone attacks launched by Kyiv. Around half of the drones were heading to the Russian capital, Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said.
The planned six-day ceasefire around Russian-occupied Oleshky has brought a rare and welcome stillness for civilians in the nearby city of Kherson, which is held by Ukraine and has also been wracked by the war.
