Both sides thanked US first lady Melania Trump for what the White House said was her role in helping broker the temporary ceasefire so food and medical supplies can be delivered to some 2,000 desperate people trapped in Oleshky. Pope Leo XIV also pressed for a truce.
“The parties are fully adhering to the agreements, and no violations of the ceasefire have been reported,” Ukrainian ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets said Thursday, adding that aid deliveries were due to begin the following day.
His Russian counterpart, Yana Lantratova, confirmed the truce was holding and that Russian engineers are working on demining Oleshky's roads.
“Both sides are fully honoring their commitments, and no violations have been recorded,” she said. “This allows military personnel to continue clearing roads of mines and to prepare a safe passage for the humanitarian convoy.”
Local people will also be able to evacuate, either into Russia or Ukraine, officials say. The mechanics of how that might work are unclear.
Lantratova said she and her team were on their way to Oleshky for the aid delivery, adding that the operation was five months in the making.
Russian and Ukrainian representatives met in the Belarus city of Homel on Thursday to fly together to the Kherson region, Belarus state media reported.
A volunteer from Oleshky, Ksenia Arkhipova, told The Associated Press roughly 1,000 residents have told her they want to leave the city.
She said it was important that the Ukrainian delegation was present in Oleshky because many residents fear Russian authorities would identify individuals with pro-Ukrainian views or ties to Ukraine’s military.
In the nearby city of Kherson, growing numbers of people were out on the streets as the truce held.
Nataliia Myronenko, 42, had a steady stream of customers at her coffee kiosk since early Thursday.
“Now, during the quiet, we have people at lunchtime and in the evening, which we didn’t have under the attacks,” she said. “For a while, people would race down this street because they were afraid to stop.”
The pause has brought a sense of relief, she said. “It’s a breath of freedom, when you don’t look at the sky. You keep looking at your feet because of the mines, but you’re not afraid of dying. It’s so great,” she said.
“It’s such a privilege and a joy, but we understand it will end soon.”
Moscow and Kyiv are keen to curry favor with Washington ahead of possible three-way talks next month.
American military support is vital for Ukraine, but US President Donald Trump has waived sanctions on Russia and publicly chided Zelensky, indicating he is disengaging with Kyiv.
Tankers carrying Russian diesel are sailing to the United States, and Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov is expected to attend a G20 ministerial meeting in Atlanta, Georgia, starting Friday, according to Russian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Maria Zakharova.
European leaders, on the other hand, have been trying to diplomatically isolate Russian President Vladimir Putin over Moscow’s invasion and what they call a campaign of sabotage across the continent.
Ukraine earlier this month reported sudden and unexpected limits on Starshield, the military-grade version of the Starlink satellite internet service owned by Elon Musk’s SpaceX that is the backbone of Ukraine’s drone operations and communications.
Putin said Russia has been in contact with the American tech titan to coordinate their orbiting activities because it is building its own equivalent of Starlink.
“Elon Musk is a genius. Truly, a real genius,” Putin said late Wednesday.
“We and our American partners value this relationship, and despite all the political issues, we continue to work closely together,” he added.

articles.title: Kim Jong Un urges drone dominance as North Korea fires missiles, rockets
articles.body:
SEOUL, Oct 30 (Reuters) - North Korean leader Kim Jong Un called for his country to seize “absolute superiority” in drone technology, speaking at an unmanned aeronautical technology exhibition and weapons demonstration, state media KCNA reported on Friday.
A firepower demonstration following the exhibition involved tactical suicide attack drones, tactical cruise missiles, multipurpose drones and a battalion of 600mm multiple rocket launchers, KCNA said.
South Korea’s military said on Thursday that North Korea had fired around 10 projectiles, including short-range ballistic missiles.
According to KCNA, Kim said that pursuing superiority in drone technology was “an indispensable option” given the changing nature of modern warfare.
He also said using high-level AI in unmanned weapons systems should be a top priority for North Korea in building modern armed forces, KCNA reported.
Kim has made repeated calls for the development of drones and AI in the military. According to state media, Kim ordered mass production of suicide attack drones in November 2024 and oversaw tests of AI-equipped versions in March 2025. In September 2025, he called AI a top priority in modernising weapons.
Since October 2024, North Korea has sent more than 16,000 personnel to Russia to aid in its war against Ukraine, and gained live experience of drone, electronic and combined-arms warfare, according to South Korean intelligence.
(Reporting by Joyce Lee; Editing by Nia Williams and Jamie Freed)

articles.title: India objects to US upgrade of Pakistani F-16s
articles.body:
India objects to US upgrade of Pakistani F-16s
India has raised objections to a $686 million US package to upgrade Pakistan’s F-16 fighter jets and extend their service life, Indian media have reported.
Washington has gone ahead with the upgrade even as India and the US continue to deepen defense cooperation under a ten-year partnership framework signed last year. India and Pakistan, both nuclear-armed, clashed briefly last year with drones and missiles following a terror attack in Jammu and Kashmir that killed 26 civilians.
Indian Defense Minister Rajnath Singh, in his talks with US Secretary of War Pete Hegseth on Wednesday, also raised the possibility of sensitive American military technology supplied to Pakistan reaching third countries, the Economic Times reported, citing officials familiar with the discussions. The two officials met on the sidelines of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Defense Ministers’ Meeting-Plus in Cebu, Philippines.
The proposed package, notified to the US Congress in December, is intended to modernize Pakistan’s aging F-16 fleet and extend their operational life through 2040.
It includes 92 Link-16 tactical communication systems, avionics upgrades, secure communications, navigation equipment, spare parts, and training, according to a US Defense Security Cooperation Agency notification published last month. The package does not involve the sale of new fighter jets, and the US agency said it would not alter the basic military balance in the region.

He also offered to share that experience with ASEAN partners through joint drills and intelligence sharing.
— RT_India (@RT_India_news) October 29, 2026
Washington has maintained that the upgrades would support cooperation with Pakistan in counterterrorism operations, improve coordination between the two countries’ air forces, and address aircraft safety concerns.
India has previously objected to American support for Pakistan’s F-16 fleet, including in 2022 when Washington approved a $450 million maintenance package. Indian Foreign Minister S. Jaishankar also questioned Washington’s justification that the aircraft were needed for counterterrorism operations.
During Wednesday’s meeting, the two sides reviewed progress on military coordination, technology sharing, and defense production, according to India’s Defense Ministry. Its public statement did not mention the F-16 objection.
Singh called for a zero-tolerance approach toward nations supporting, training, or financing terrorist organizations, and Hegseth reaffirmed Washington’s support for India in combating cross-border terrorism.
Both ministers agreed to strengthen military exchanges, maritime security cooperation, and defense supply chains, with Singh describing the India-US partnership as a cornerstone of a free, open, and secure Indo-Pacific.

articles.title: North Korea fires 'around a dozen' ballistic missiles into Sea of Japan: Seoul
articles.body:
North Korea fired "around a dozen" short-range ballistic missiles off its east coast on Thursday, Seoul's defence ministry said, less than a week after South Korea proposed talks over a growing border row.
South Korea's Joint Chiefs of Staff (JCS) said its military detected "around a dozen short-range ballistic missiles fired from the Wonsan area of North Korea towards the East Sea", the body of water also known as the Sea of Japan.
"Our military has stepped up surveillance and vigilance against possible additional launches," it added in its statement.
The Japan Coast Guard separately said that "an object that appears to be a ballistic missile launched from North Korea seems to have already fallen", urging ships to be vigilant.
North Korea has tested a slew of weapons recently, including a new precision-guided torpedo system and an intermediate-range hypersonic missile, both of which were said to employ AI technology.
Thursday's flurry of missiles comes against the backdrop of growing tensions over a landmine explosion along the heavily fortified border between the two Koreas that saw three South Korean soldiers wounded.
A joint Seoul-UN investigation earlier this month concluded that North Korea planted the landmines over a year ago.
Seoul accused Pyongyang of "a clear violation of the Armistice Agreement" and called for the North to return to dialogue.
No response
Pyongyang has since ridiculed South Korean President Lee Jae-myung's overture, with Kim Yo-jong, the powerful sister of the North's leader, dubbing it "the climax of the farce".
Last week, South Korea proposed military talks with the North to "mutually confirm the precise location" of their border and discuss restoring communication channels, but Pyongyang has yet to respond.
The DMZ is one of the world's most heavily fortified frontiers, and landmine incidents have previously heightened tensions between the two countries.
Seoul and Pyongyang remain technically at war, as the Korean conflict ended in 1953 with a truce rather than a peace treaty.
The ratcheting tensions come as US President Donald Trump's recent overtures to North Korea have raised concerns that Seoul, an ally of Washington, could be sidelined in potential nuclear talks involving Pyongyang.
In his most recent comments, Trump seemingly downplayed the possibility of a summit while insisting his relationship with North Korean leader Kim Jong-un is "very good".
In October, North Korea launched several short-range ballistic missiles a day after Trump suggested the two might meet this year.

articles.title: PM Radev Says Bulgaria Was Ready to Deploy Jets Against the Black Sea Drones
articles.body:
PM Radev Says Bulgaria Was Ready to Deploy Jets Against the Black Sea Drones
Prime Minister Rumen Radev said Bulgaria was ready to deploy L-39 military aircraft against drones that attacked a commercial vessel in the Black Sea if the unmanned aerial vehicles had entered the country's territorial waters, adding that a French patrol aircraft had detected them at least 30 minutes before the strike.
The Bulgarian Air Force had L-39 aircraft stationed in Balchik on standby for a possible response, Radev said as he discussed the recent Black Sea incidents and Bulgaria's ability to counter such threats.
Radev said authorities had obtained video footage of the attack and were examining it in cooperation with allied intelligence services. Forensic analyses are also underway to establish where the drones originated.
“We have video footage, which we have shared with our allies. Every possible analysis is currently being conducted. I expect that we will finally have clear evidence as to where these drones came from,” Radev said.
The prime minister added that the footage would be released publicly as soon as possible, but stressed that he could not yet identify those responsible for the attack.
“We do not yet know where the drone originated. I have shared my logical assumptions with you, but I do not wish to jump to conclusions. I imagine you have seen discussions on social media, where all sorts of theories are circulating - suggesting, for instance, that the drone could belong to any of four or five different countries. However, such claims are not to be taken seriously. We intend to conduct a thorough and credible expert assessment in collaboration with our allies,” Radev said.
He described the coordination between the Bulgarian Armed Forces and allied aircraft conducting patrols over the Black Sea, saying a French reconnaissance plane had spotted the drones in time to warn the targeted ship's crew.
“We have been in constant communication with NATO, requesting assistance. As you know, there are already aircraft on patrol, including American ones. In fact, the French patrol aircraft spotted the drones at least half an hour before the strike; it detected them and even provided information on their trajectory. This gave the crew of the targeted ship the opportunity to take all necessary evacuation measures,” the prime minister said.
Radev said allied forces and the Bulgarian military were exchanging information in real time. He reiterated that Bulgaria had been prepared to respond militarily if the drones had entered its territorial waters.
“We were prepared to scramble L-39 aircraft based in Balchik and use their weaponry against these drones, had they entered our territorial waters. But it didn't come to that,” he said.
However, Radev warned that Bulgaria's response options were subject to legal and practical restrictions. International law prevents the country from taking military action outside its own territorial waters, while weather, available equipment, and surveillance capabilities also limit its ability to detect and respond to threats in the exclusive economic zone.
“Even if we possess the means to intervene, we cannot, from a strictly legal standpoint, take action outside our own territorial zones. We cannot do so, as it would constitute a violation of international law. Furthermore, there are various limitations regarding the capabilities at our disposal for surveillance, reconnaissance, and the detection of threats within the Exclusive Economic Zone,” Radev said.
He also pointed to Bulgaria's limited naval capacity, which prevents it from maintaining a permanent presence across the entire zone.
“Moreover, we are dependent on weather conditions. It is not always possible to fly, nor is it always possible to take action. Our fleet is limited in both number and capabilities. We are unable to maintain a continuous watch across the entire Exclusive Economic Zone,” the prime minister said.
Radev seeks additional NATO assistance
Radev confirmed that he had discussed the need for further allied support with NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte.
“We are waiting. I have also raised this issue with Mark Rutte. You can see that the quantities of weaponry available to NATO also have their limits. They are stretched from the Baltic Sea, across the land, to the Black Sea. So, everything that can be done is being done,” he said.
Bulgaria has also pursued diplomatic action at the highest international level, including through the United Nations, NATO, and European institutions, Radev said. He argued that military measures and allied assistance could reduce risks but would not ensure that attacks on ships stopped.
“From this point on, there is only one solution to ensure that these attacks finally come to an end: a ceasefire, sitting down at the negotiating table, and beginning talks. Until that happens, there is no guarantee regarding what can be done,” Radev said.
He said the European Union and NATO should support diplomatic initiatives aimed at ending hostilities, citing efforts to open talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin, including those by Finnish President Alexander Stubb and the Norwegian prime minister.
“The only 100% guarantee is a ceasefire and the political will for dialogue. I believe the European Union and NATO should engage in these efforts,” Radev said.
The prime minister also pledged formal diplomatic action if expert assessments establish the drones' origin and responsibility for the attack.
“If the origin of these drones is proven, the Minister of Foreign Affairs will immediately summon the relevant ambassador to deliver a note of protest,” Radev said.
Three drones struck a vessel 16 nautical miles off Cape Kaliakra, and its crew was rescued. The incident involved the merchant ship CONTSHIP JET, which was hit on October 28 about 16 nautical miles from the cape. Although the crew survived, the vessel was reported to have sunk the following day.
The attack has renewed concerns about the safety of commercial shipping in the Black Sea and the risks to trade routes close to Bulgarian territorial waters.
The European Commission also reacted to the attacks on civilian vessels, calling them an “unacceptable escalation” that threatens EU interests, maritime transport, and supply chains. Brussels expressed solidarity with Bulgaria and Romania, warning that the consequences of the war in Ukraine continued to pose serious security risks in the Black Sea region.
Radev contrasts Bulgaria's response with Romania's
Radev defended Bulgaria's decision not to identify a country as responsible for the drone attacks before conclusive evidence was available. He cited Romania, which he said had blamed Russia but subsequently experienced another incident.
“Bulgaria did not make definitive accusations against any country because we lacked concrete evidence at the time. Romania stated that the aggressor and the source of these drones was Russia. Yet, this failed to protect them. The very next day, drones sank a ship—within their own territorial waters, no less. Do you see the difference?” Radev said.
He criticized Bulgarian politicians calling for the immediate naming of a suspected perpetrator, arguing that public accusations would not prevent further attacks.
“I want to address all our politicians who so convincingly propagate the notion that if we speak out and declare, 'You, Russia, are the source of the attack', if we shake our finger at them, that will protect us. It cannot protect us. Look at what happened in Romania: the very next day, a ship was struck and sunk. And I repeat - this did not happen in the exclusive economic zone, but in territorial waters,” the prime minister said.
Radev says government will follow court ruling on CEC complaint
Radev also commented on a Central Election Commission (CEC) decision concerning a complaint against him over his support for Iliyana Yotova's candidacy, which had been expressed through the government press office.
He said the Council of Ministers would comply with the commission's decision, while noting that the final course of action would depend on the court because the ruling had been appealed.
“The Council of Ministers will comply with the decision of the Central Election Commission. Whatever the Bulgarian court decides, that is what we will do,” Radev said.

articles.title: Purges at the Pentagon: Hegseth fires top military planner
articles.body:
Purges at the Pentagon: Hegseth fires top military planner
Kyiv • UNN
Lieutenant General Brett Sylvia was removed from his position as director of J5 without an immediate replacement. The dismissal came amid possible U.S. strikes on Iran.
U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth fired the Pentagon’s top military planner. A Pentagon representative said this on October 28, UNN reports, citing AP.
Details
This is the latest in a series of generals being dismissed, and it comes even as U.S. President Donald Trump is considering resuming strikes on Iran in the eight-month war.
U.S. Army Lieutenant General Brett Sylvia was removed as head of the Strategy, Plans and Policy Directorate of the U.S. Joint Chiefs of Staff. He became the second general dismissed from the position, known in military circles as "J5," under Hegseth. His predecessor, Lieutenant General Joseph McGee, was forced to retire in October last year.
A Pentagon representative said there was no immediate replacement for Sylvia and that no reason for his dismissal had been provided.
A representative of the U.S. Joint Chiefs of Staff said: "The Chairman, Joint Staff and Joint Force express their deep gratitude to Lieutenant General Brett Sylvia and his family for 32 years of distinguished service to our country" and "wish him and his family all the best."
Typically, the J5 director and his staff are responsible for developing and coordinating military plans with both the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff and the U.S. president. Sylvia’s dismissal came amid Trump’s repeated statements about launching new military operations against Iran.
Trump vowed to "finish what was started" in Iran after the war with Israel began eight months ago and said new strikes could take place after next week’s midterm elections.
According to two diplomats familiar with the situation, U.S. officials warned a number of Middle Eastern countries and regional allies that they needed to be prepared for the possible resumption of hostilities after Tuesday’s election, as well as possible retaliatory measures by Iran. They said Trump had not yet made a final decision on new strikes.
A third U.S. aircraft carrier and thousands of additional troops are heading to the region.

Last month, Hegseth said he had ordered the reduction in the total number of senior officer positions to be doubled to 20%, to be completed by January 1, 2027. There are currently about 800 admiral and general positions.
Some members of Congress have criticized the reduction in the number of general officers as a "purge" that will take years to recover from.
"He has some deeply rooted resentment toward the leadership in the Army. He is getting rid of an entire generation of great Army leaders, and it will take a whole generation to recover from this," Democratic Senator Mark Kelly, a former U.S. Navy combat pilot who has criticized Hegseth, said last month.

articles.title: Fire breaks out at US nuclear weapons facility
articles.body:
Fire breaks out at US nuclear weapons facility
A fire broke out at a major nuclear research complex in South Carolina that supports the US nuclear weapons program, the Department of Energy has said.
The fire started at Savannah River National Laboratory, part of the Savannah River Site (SRS) near Aiken, on Wednesday evening and was subsequently extinguished, officials said.
“No contamination has been reported outside the affected facility,” the department said in a statement.
Emergency protocols were activated, with employees not involved in response efforts ordered to suspend operations and shelter in place as a precaution. The site was closed to incoming traffic, while nearby rail, river, and air traffic was restricted.
Officials lifted the emergency declaration at 9:45 PM, saying radiation surveys found no detectable contamination. Protective measures were lifted, and the site was cleared to resume normal operations on Thursday.
Local media reported that the fire broke out in a single room and involved an unfiltered, ground-level radiological release. One employee was reportedly hospitalized with minor injuries.
Established in the early 1950s during the Cold War, the SRS originally produced plutonium and tritium for US nuclear weapons. Although its production reactors have since been shut down, the complex continues to play a key role in maintaining the American nuclear arsenal.
The SRS processes and replenishes tritium, a radioactive isotope of hydrogen used to boost the explosive yield of nuclear warheads. It also manages nuclear materials, treats radioactive waste, and carries out environmental cleanup.
The US government is also developing a facility at the SRS to manufacture plutonium cores for nuclear warheads as part of efforts to modernize the country’s nuclear weapons stockpile.
The incident comes less than two weeks after a fire swept through Canadian Forces Base Wainwright in Alberta, killing four soldiers and injuring 39 others during a live-fire training exercise. According to the Canadian military, strong winds caused the fire to spread rapidly, overtaking an area occupied by troops.
The Canadian Armed Forces said last week that 27 personnel remained hospitalized, while 12 were discharged. Military police have launched an independent investigation into the incident.

articles.title: Trump receives rare Iran strike briefing as US weighs renewed war
articles.body:
The top U.S. military commander in the Middle East presented President Donald Trump with options for renewed strikes against Iran during an unusual face-to-face meeting at the White House on Thursday, as Washington considers launching another major military campaign against Tehran, The Wall Street Journal reported, citing U.S. officials and others with direct knowledge of the discussions.
Adm. Brad Cooper, commander of U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM), was joined by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff Gen. Dan Caine and other Cabinet officials. The meeting also covered matters beyond Iran, according to the report.
Cooper rarely briefs Trump in person, making Thursday's meeting particularly significant as the U.S. military prepares for the possibility of renewed fighting. The admiral previously met Trump in July, when he joined Hegseth and Caine aboard Air Force One in Delaware. The Journal said the unusual visit could indicate that Washington is moving closer to significant military operations.
The meeting followed discussions at the White House on Wednesday, when senior military officers met Vice President JD Vance. At the same time, the administration has continued efforts to reopen diplomatic channels with Tehran. The Journal previously reported that Vance had reached out to a senior Iranian hardliner in an attempt to revive negotiations.
The diplomatic contacts are taking place alongside preparations for a possible military confrontation. According to earlier reporting by the Journal, Trump administration officials have advised Arab Gulf countries to prepare for a short but intense military campaign following the U.S. midterm elections next week.
The Pentagon has also increased its military presence and defensive capabilities in the Middle East in recent weeks, sending additional air defense systems, ammunition and supplies to the region. U.S. forces have been relocated from certain bases considered particularly vulnerable to Iranian retaliation, according to the report.
Trump himself raised the possibility of renewed military action during a rally last week, referring to the major U.S.-Israeli bombing campaign against Iran earlier this year, known as Operation Epic Fury.
"We may do another little Epic Fury," Trump said. "Or they'll agree."
Iran, meanwhile, has warned both publicly and through private diplomatic communications that it would respond to any new American attack by striking U.S. military positions and targets in Gulf countries.
According to the Journal, Tehran has also resumed producing ballistic missiles using components stored in underground facilities and intensified efforts to target American personnel stationed across the Middle East.
The possibility of another military campaign has raised concerns among some lawmakers in Washington. Sen. Chris Murphy, a Connecticut Democrat who said he had previously received classified briefings on some of the planning, sharply criticized the prospect of renewed hostilities.
Speaking Wednesday at the Middle East Institute, Murphy described the plans as "insane."
"It will lead to devastating escalation and the likely destruction of our commitment to the rule of law," he said.
A Pentagon spokesperson and a spokesperson for CENTCOM declined to comment on the White House meeting, according to the Journal. While the administration continues to examine military options, the renewed diplomatic contacts and regional military preparations leave open whether Trump will pursue another agreement with Tehran or authorize a new round of strikes.

articles.title: Gulf War Air Campaign Map Featured in New Smithsonian Exhibit
articles.body:
A map pinned to the wall in a basement 36 years ago will go on display in November at the Smithsonian’s National Air and Space Museum.
The map, used to identify strategic targets across Iraq in the fall of 1990, was used in the planning of Operation Desert Storm, and will be included in the museum’s new “Modern Military Aviation” gallery in Washington D.C., tracing advances in airpower from the Korean War to the present.
The exhibit seeks to expose visitors to the advances that changed the nature of warfare.
The map is one of two created at the time by now-retired Lt. Gen. David Deptula, Dean of the Mitchell Institute for Aerospace Studies. Deptula was the principal air attack planner for Operation Desert Storm—identifying strategic targets across Iraq and developing the blueprint for the coalition air campaign.
Two Gulf War maps remain in Deptula’s possession, and both are on display at AFA’s headquarters in Arlington: one depicting Baghdad hangs in AFA’s Heritage Hall, while a larger map of Iraq hangs in Deptula’s office, surrounded by other mementos and artifacts from throughout his career.
A reproduction of the map will be displayed as a large-format graphic panel at the Smithsonian. Dr. Michael Hankins, the Smithsonian’s Curator of U.S. Air Force, Navy, and Marine Corps post-World War II Aviation, learned about the maps during a chance conversation with the Mitchell Institute’s Executive Director Doug Birkey. Hankins was aware the maps had existed, but did not know they had been carried back from Saudi Arabia after the war.
Hankins immediately recognized the narrative the maps could tell and saw them as a perfect bridge for the exhibit he was creating, one that could help tell the story of the evolution from conventional airpower to the age of stealth and precision bombing that has defined military strike operations ever since.
Given the map’s fragility and size, Hankins decided a reproduction would be more accessible to visitors at the Smithsonian.
“As we were planning the layouts for some of these different labels, we had an opportunity, particularly in that section, to have a large-scale photo as an introduction to the Desert Storm section of the gallery,” Hankins said. “What better visual image to use than this to speak to that? … [It shows] how the thought process of using military aviation was different in 1991 than it might have been in previous conflicts.”
The Map, Deptula, and the Black Hole
While the map tells the story of Operation Desert Storm, it is also a pivotal artifact in the career of the officer who led the planning of that operation over countless 20-hour days in a basement room in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, that came to be known as “the Black Hole.” On Aug. 2, 1990, Iraqi forces under dictator Saddam Hussein invaded neighboring Kuwait and conquered the country within days. In response, a coalition led by the United States was formed to eject Saddam’s forces from Kuwait.
Deptula, then a lieutenant colonel working in the Office of the Secretary of the Air Force, was pulled into a Pentagon strategic planning cell known as “Checkmate,” led by Col. John Warden III. The Checkmate team had been developing a new strategic air doctrine for the post-Cold War era when it was tasked to create an operational concept for countering Iraq’s invasion with airpower. They dubbed their plan “Instant Thunder.” After briefing Army Gen. Norman Schwarzkopf, who as commander of U.S. Central Command would oversee the operation, as well as Gen. Colin Powell, then the Chairman of the Joint Chiefs, Warden, Deptula and a couple of others flew to Saudi Arabia to brief Gen. Chuck Horner, the top air commander for the theater, on the plan.
Horner, unconvinced of Warden’s ability to lead the actual planning, accepted Warden’s concept, but sent Warden back to Washington, while retaining the others. Among them, only Deptula stayed long term, becoming the principal target planner for the entire campaign.
Based in the Royal Saudi Air Force headquarters basement, their “Black Hole” office was defined by secrecy, the sensitive political nature of American forces planning offensive operations on Saudi soil, and the punishing hours demanded of its occupants—and, Deptula recalled, once “someone was allowed to come into it, they were never allowed to go out.”
Here Deptula created his map and the Master Air Attack Plan that would ultimately orchestrate every strike of the campaign. On the map, Deptula and his team pinpointed strategic targets, coded by category: air defense, leadership, military bases, Scud ballistic missile launchers, command and control systems, and electricity and telecommunications networks.
The map helped planners to identify relationships between targets, coordinate force packages across multiple objectives simultaneously, and find gaps in Iraqi defenses that a list of coordinates alone could not reveal. For example, the map revealed a gap in Iraqi border monitoring stations that allowed Deptula to safely route F-15E attack aircraft to strike Scud launchers in western Iraq before they could fire on Israel. “It wasn’t just a pretty map that hung on the wall in our planning cell,” Deptula said. “That’s what the visualization of a map does that a bunch of target coordinates and names doesn’t.”
Underlying the Instant Thunder concept was the conviction that airpower could systematically dismantle Iraq’s war-making ability. Each mark aimed to take a specific capability off the table. It was a deliberate break from what Deptula called “an attritional, intelligence-based philosophy” that had defined air campaigns in Vietnam, where success was measured by the percentage of damage inflicted rather than by what capability had actually been removed.
Using the F-117 Nighthawk’s stealth capability to lead the attack, and precision munitions to ensure rapid success, coalition air forces disabled Iraq’s command and control almost instantly, and took away other war-making capabilities within weeks—all while greatly minimizing overall infrastructure damage across the country.
By targeting electrical transformer yards, rather than power plants, planners saw they could shut down the electrical grid while keeping reconstruction manageable. In some cases, Deptula recalled, Iraqi power plant managers switched off their facilities, and the coalition chose not to strike them.
“By the third night of the war, there hadn’t been an electron flowing in the Iraqi power grid,” said Deptula. “So that’s the objective.” For Hankins, the map illustrated the evolution of airpower in a way no other artifact could. He said, “I think the map shows that in an interesting way, because you can see who’s targeting what, what kinds of things they are able to target, what kinds of things they were successful at. It’s different than something you would see in the sections on the Korean War or the Vietnam War.”
Serving as the visual introduction, the map opens the gallery’s Desert Storm section, which focuses on the new technologies that defined the conflict: a scale model of an F-117 stealth fighter and an interactive display explaining how stealth technology works and why it proved so decisive.
Separately, the museum’s Steven F. Udvar-Hazy Center near Dulles Airport received an original F-117 in October, so Washington visitors can see the real thing up close.
The Desert Storm section will also serve as a bridge to the conflicts of the Global War on Terror that the United States has fought over the past three decades, including the Predator drone Deptula would later help pioneer as an armed platform. After the September 11 attacks, Deptula was directing the Combined Air Operations Center for the opening of the Afghanistan campaign when the United States fired a Hellfire missile from an RQ-1 Predator at al-Qaeda targets, the first combat use of an armed remotely piloted aircraft.
For Deptula, the map’s display at the Smithsonian represents an acknowledgment of a turning point in how America wages war and as validation of the campaign itself. “I think it’s recognition of the significance of the operation,” Deptula said. “It was the birth of how we conceive air operations.”
For Hankins, the map’s greatest value may be what it teaches visitors who know nothing about the Gulf War. “It’s not just let’s launch a bunch of airplanes and go drop a bunch of weapons,” he said. “It’s much more careful than that. It takes a lot of people a lot of time.”
The Modern Military Aviation gallery, the final chapter of the Smithsonian’s eight-year renovation, is scheduled to open to the public on Veterans Day, Nov. 11, 2026.

articles.title: North Korea launches missile salvo toward the Sea of Japan
articles.body:
- North Korea launched suspected ballistic missiles at about 12:36 p.m. on Oct. 29, Japan said, with nothing reaching its territory or exclusive economic zone.
- South Korea said around 10 short-range ballistic missiles were fired from the Wonsan area, North Korea’s first ballistic launch in 17 days.
North Korea launched what may have been a ballistic missile at about 12:36 p.m. local time on Oct. 29, and it is presumed to have fallen near the east coast of the Korean Peninsula without reaching Japan’s territory or exclusive economic zone, Japan’s Ministry of Defense said on social media.
Tokyo said Japan, the United States and South Korea are working closely to analyze the launch, and that so far there have been no reports of damage to aircraft or ships operating nearby. The exclusive economic zone is the band of sea extending up to 200 nautical miles (370 km) from Japan’s coast, where Tokyo controls fishing and resources.
Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi was briefed immediately and gave three instructions: gather and analyze information and keep the public quickly and accurately informed, thoroughly confirm the safety of aircraft and ships, and prepare for any contingency. The government’s North Korea task force at the prime minister’s crisis management center pulled together information from ministries and convened an emergency team to discuss the response.
Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi then ordered the Self-Defense Forces to work closely with the United States and South Korea on collecting and analyzing information and to keep up surveillance in case of further developments. The Japanese government said North Korea’s repeated missile launches threaten the peace and security of Japan, the region and the international community, and it promised to release more details as they become available.
South Korea’s Joint Chiefs of Staff gave a fuller picture, saying North Korea fired around 10 short-range ballistic missiles from the Wonsan area on its east coast toward the sea at about 12:30 p.m., SBS reported. Neither government has yet said how far the missiles flew or how high they climbed, and North Korean state media had not commented on the launch by Thursday afternoon.
The launch is North Korea’s first ballistic missile firing in 17 days and follows a busy October. On Oct. 3, it fired a missile from near its east coast that Japan’s Defense Ministry said flew about 680 km (420 miles) at a peak altitude of about 90 km (56 miles) before landing outside Japan’s exclusive economic zone. On Oct. 12, Pyongyang fired several ballistic missiles from near its capital, some of which flew more than 900 km (560 miles), and later called them tactical ballistic missiles, short-range weapons meant for battlefield targets. Two days later, it test-fired two types of submarine-launched strategic cruise missiles in the sea east of the peninsula.
The launches come as tensions remain high along the inter-Korean border. In early October, South Korea and the U.S.-led United Nations Command concluded that North Korea had deliberately planted the mines that wounded three South Korean soldiers inside the Demilitarized Zone on Sept. 21. South Korea’s National Security Office held an emergency meeting after Thursday’s launch and said the repeated ballistic missile firings violate United Nations Security Council resolutions, which bar North Korea from testing ballistic missiles.

articles.title: Ukraine destroys 2 Russian Su-34 bomber jets in Neptune missile strike on airfield, Navy says
articles.body:
Ukraine destroys 2 Russian Su-34 bomber jets in Neptune missile strike on airfield, Navy says
Ukraine's Navy destroyed two Russian Su-34 fighter-bomber jets in a strike against the Marinovka military airfield in Russia's Volgograd Oblast, using domestically produced Neptune missiles, the Navy reported on Oct. 29.
The aircraft were destroyed at the base of Russia's 11th Mixed Aviation Regiment near the settlement of Oktyabrsky, according to the Navy. The regiment belongs to the 4th Mixed Aviation Division of Russia's 4th Air and Air Defense Forces Army. The Navy did not provide any visual confirmation of the strike. The Kyiv Independent could not independently verify the claim.
Later on Oct. 29, President Volodymyr Zelensky confirmed the destruction of the two Su-34 jets, adding that Ukrainian forces had also hit a Russian Iskander missile launcher.
The Su-34 is one of Russia's main aircraft used to launch guided aerial bombs against Ukrainian cities, frontline settlements, and military positions. Strikes against these aircraft could weaken Russia's ability to carry out such attacks, while replacing the losses requires significant time and resources.
Russia had approximately 140 Su-34 fighter-bombers of various modifications in service as of Oct. 22, including the modernized Su-34M, Ukraine's military intelligence agency (HUR) reported on Oct. 29.
According to the agency, Russia has lost 43 Su-34 aircraft destroyed and another seven damaged since the start of its full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
"Such losses are quite significant for the aggressor's aircraft fleet, whose restoration requires a lengthy production cycle, substantial financial resources, and specialized industrial cooperation," HUR said.
The agency estimated that Russia can manufacture approximately 14 to 18 Su-34 aircraft annually, meaning the number of destroyed aircraft is equivalent to roughly 2.5–3 years of production.
Despite the losses, Russia continues to manufacture and modernize the aircraft to maintain its fleet and sustain aerial attacks against Ukraine.
The latest strike follows an Oct. 15 attack on the Borisoglebsk military airfield in Russia's Voronezh Oblast that destroyed four Su-34M bomber-jets and damaged two more. The attack was also carried out using Neptune missiles.
The Ukrainian ground-launched Neptune cruise missile is best known for sinking Russia's Black Sea flagship, the Moskva, in 2022. Ukraine has since developed a longer-range version capable of striking targets up to 1,000 kilometers (620 miles) away.

articles.title: Ship Sinks After Drone Strike in Bulgaria's Economic Zone as Defense Chief Says "It Came from the East"
articles.body:
Outgoing Chief of Defense Admiral Emil Eftimov told bTV that the maritime drones that struck the container ship CONTSHIP JET near Cape Kaliakra came from the east, while emphasizing that Bulgaria’s military had intelligence about a possible attack and that legal restrictions prevented it from engaging the drones outside the country’s territorial waters.
"Yesterday's drones came from the direction of the sea - from the east," Eftimov said, adding that the armed forces had sufficient information about the unmanned vehicles but did not publicly attribute the attack to a specific country.
He said the military had received advance intelligence about a potential strike and had taken precautions. "We had information, which is why we took appropriate measures. Following the incident in Kardam and the strikes that occurred in early October, this represents a consistent intensification of our efforts - specifically regarding reconnaissance, surveillance, situational analysis, and early warning, which is what took place yesterday," he said.
Asked whether Russia was responsible, Eftimov declined to make a definitive attribution. "I have not heard any Chief of Defense, whether from Romania, Turkey, or any other nation, offer a categorical assessment regarding the origin or attribution of such malicious acts based on the professional intelligence available to them." He said Bulgaria operates as a NATO member and follows the Alliance’s Strategic Concept.
Eftimov said the armed forces had responded appropriately and rejected criticism that Bulgaria had failed to act. Since August, the country has strengthened its air defense and surveillance systems and expanded its air force capabilities, including Su-25, L-39 and F-16 aircraft.
He explained that Bulgaria strictly observes international law and is authorized to engage threats only within its territorial waters. "Do we operate outside our territorial waters? No. We lack the mandate to do so," he said.
Severe weather also hindered the deployment of interceptor assets, although aviation units remained on standby. The drones did not enter Bulgarian territorial waters, where the armed forces would have been able to engage them, Eftimov said. He stressed that Bulgaria was not at war and that the measures taken amounted to stronger security efforts rather than an escalation.
The CONTSHIP JET, a Liberian-flagged container ship sailing from Haifa, Israel, to Constanța, Romania, sank around midnight east of Varna, according to maritime news outlets and the regional administration. It had been struck by three maritime drones on October 28 within Bulgaria’s exclusive economic zone, about 21 nautical miles southeast of Shabla.
The attack caused a fire and severe damage to the vessel’s starboard side, leaving it listing heavily. All 18 crew members were evacuated onto life rafts and rescued without fatalities or injuries, but the damage proved too extensive for the ship to be stabilized, and it sank overnight into Thursday.
The incident was the fifth attack on a vessel within Bulgaria’s exclusive economic zone. Speaking to Bulgarian National Radio (BNR), shipping agency owner Captain Todor Georgiev said the drones were Russian and described the attack as "a mockery of [Russia's] Black Sea neighbors."
Separately, the Council of Ministers has proposed that the Bulgarian president issue a decree relieving Eftimov of his position as Chief of Defense and discharging him from military service effective January 2, 2027. The proposal follows a formal request from the admiral under Article 163 of the Defense and Armed Forces of the Republic of Bulgaria Act.
Eftimov submitted his request to leave military service on September 30, 2026, with three months’ notice. At the time, he was expected to remain in office until the end of the year.
He has led Bulgaria’s defense establishment since March 2020, following a career in the Naval Forces, the Defense Ministry and NATO structures. In December 2023, the Council of Ministers proposed extending his tenure after his initial four-year term expired. The extension took effect on March 31, 2024.
Born in Varna on August 16, 1961, Eftimov graduated from the N. Y. Vaptsarov Naval Academy in 1984 and subsequently held various command and staff positions in the Naval Forces. He served as commander of the Varna Naval Base and worked at NATO’s International Military Staff in Brussels from 2011 to 2016.
He became deputy chief of defense in 2016 and briefly served as acting chief of defense in early 2017, before returning to the deputy position. He was appointed head of the Bulgarian Armed Forces in March 2020 and received the rank of admiral that same year.
During the final months of his tenure, Eftimov continued to represent Bulgaria’s military leadership in NATO defense policy initiatives and allied commitments. In September 2026, he stressed the need to balance the rapid adoption of innovations with maintaining interoperability. Earlier in the year, he highlighted the importance of NATO’s regional defense plans for security in the Black Sea region.
His departure is to be formalized by presidential decree. Under the proposed timeline, Eftimov will leave office after more than six years as chief of defense and over four decades of military service.

articles.title: Merz stated that military cooperation between Russia and North Korea threatens Europe's security
articles.body:
Merz stated that military cooperation between Russia and North Korea threatens Europe's security
Kyiv • UNN
Merz stated that North Korean troops in the war against Ukraine threaten Europe's freedom. Germany and South Korea will deepen security cooperation.
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said on Thursday that North Korea threatens "freedom throughout Europe" by sending its troops to fight on Russia’s side in the war against Ukraine. This was reported by DW, writes UNN.
Details
After a meeting in Seoul with South Korean President Lee Jae-myung, Merz emphasized that Russia supplies weapons to North Korea.
The chancellor said that such cooperation demonstrates how "the security of Korea affects the security of Europe. And the security of Europe also affects the security of Korea."
It is noted that North Korea has strengthened its military ties with Russia since the start of the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
Pyongyang supplied Moscow with artillery ammunition and missiles. In addition, according to South Korean intelligence services, it sent about 15,000 troops to participate in combat operations on the side of Russian forces.
In return, Russia provides North Korea with financial support, military technologies, and security guarantees.
Before Merz’s arrival on Thursday, North Korea launched about 10 short-range ballistic missiles toward the Sea of Japan, the South Korean military reported.
At the beginning of his visit, Merz said he hoped for the future reunification of Korea. The peninsula has been divided along the 38th parallel since the end of the fighting in the Korean War in 1953.
Merz also agreed with Lee to deepen strategic and security cooperation between the two countries. This includes joint military exercises and the exchange of intelligence information.

Ukraine Teams Up With the Netherlands for Next-Gen Air Defense Project Bliksem
The Ukrainian and Dutch defense sectors have started working on a joint air defense initiative named Bliksem.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy reported the initiative on X on October 28.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The task was issued to teams from both countries following discussions between Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten during a visit to the Netherlands.
The leaders met with representatives from Ukrainian and Dutch defense, energy, and software firms to outline key priorities for economic and technical cooperation.
During the visit, both leaders identified focus areas to strengthen industrial and technological ties between the two nations. These priorities include military manufacturing, energy ventures, satellite technologies, and air defense capabilities amid Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
“Our teams have a task to work out a specific project in the field of air defense – Bliksem. We have already started this work. We are bringing our cooperation to a level where being alongside Ukraine means receiving additional industrial, technological, and social positive results,” stated Zelenskyy.
Previously, the Netherlands announced a €500 million ($543 million) military aid package for Ukraine focused on strengthening its air defense capabilities with American-made systems.
This decision made the Netherlands the first NATO member to directly finance US weapons, specifically supplying components and missiles for the Patriot system as part of bilateral support.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy confirmed that the aid agreement resulted from a conversation with Dutch Prime Minister Dick Schoof following the NATO summit in The Hague, while Dutch Defense Minister Ruben Brekelmans emphasized the urgent need to deliver the air defense equipment amid intensifying Russian strikes.

articles.title: 'Horrific' Russian drone strike kills 13 at Ukraine train station: Kyiv
articles.body:
At least 13 killed in 'horrific' Russian drone strike at Ukraine train station
At least 13 people were killed when a Russian drone struck a busy railway station in Ukraine's Dnipro on Thursday, President Volodymyr Zelensky said, describing the attack as "horrific" and urging Kyiv's allies not to ease sanctions on Moscow.
A Russian drone slammed into a busy platform at a railway station in Ukraine's Dnipro on Thursday killing at least 13 people in what President Volodymyr Zelensky called a "horrific" attack that demands a response from Kyiv's allies.
The strike on the city located in the east of the country came as Ukraine and Russia strive to uphold a fragile local ceasefire in the ravaged city of Oleshky – which has been subject to Russian occupation since 2022 and where residents have faced months of food, water and medicine shortages.
Read moreCeasefire in Russia-occupied Ukrainian city holds for second day
The truce was holding into its third day, both countries said, with the Ukrainian human rights ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets announcing that he had "set out with the Ukrainian delegation towards Oleshky" through Belarus and Russia.

But elsewhere, Moscow continued to pummel Ukraine.
The strike hit a platform of the Dnipro train station "where a regular commuter train and a regular passenger train were standing", Zelensky said.
"Sanctions against Moscow and its war machine must not be eased for as long as this Russian war continues," he added, slamming the attack as "horrific".
Images released by Ukrainian emergency services showed bodies on the platform, rescuers helping victims to safety and two burnt-out passenger trains with their windows shattered.
Russia has fired drones at trains across Ukraine since the first days of its 2022 invasion – destroying hundreds of locomotives and killing several railway workers.
In September alone, passengers were evacuated from more than 5,800 Ukrainian train services due to the threat of Russian drone strikes, the national railway operator told AFP.
Ukraine's vast train network is a vital form of transport in the country, where journeys between east and west can take 24 hours.

Zelensky slams sanctions relief
Ukraine's air force said it had intercepted three jet-powered drones in a daytime attack, but that a fourth evaded its defences and hit the station.
The head of Ukraine Railways, Oleksandr Pertsovsky, said an elevated threat level had been announced.
"But unfortunately there were still a large number of people on the platform," he said on Facebook.
In the aftermath of the attack, Zelensky refreshed his criticism of a deal struck this month between US President Donald Trump and his Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin to ease some sanctions on Russia allowing Moscow to release diesel onto global markets.
"How many such terrorist strikes has Russia carried out against our people since sanctions were lifted on some Russian oligarchs and energy sector, instead of de-escalating," he asked.
At least five others were killed across Ukraine in separate Russian attacks, according to local officials.
Two teenagers killed
A strike on the city centre of Chernigiv, north of Kyiv, killed two 15-year-old girls and wounded more than a dozen, the head of the city's military administration, Dmytro Bryzhynsky, said.
A drone also slammed into a multi-storey residential building in the central city of Kremenchuk, killing two and wounding several – including a six-year-old – the local governor said.
Russia has intensified drone and missile attacks on Ukraine in recent weeks, hitting energy sites around major cities in what Kyiv says is a bid to plunge the country into cold and darkness throughout the winter.
The Kremlin earlier this week vowed not to let up in the overall pace of the war even as the sides prepare to restart stalled talks under US mediation.
Zelensky said on Wednesday it would be a "huge success" if the local ceasefire in Oleshky – brokered by US First Lady Melania Trump – allowed for the evacuation of stranded citizens.

Locals caught there have resorted to hunting and eating pigeons in recent months, former residents in touch with those in the city told AFP.
Russia and Ukraine are to meet next month with US envoys to discuss ways to end Europe's worst conflict since World War II, with no firm dates set for the talks yet.
Several previous rounds have failed to move the sides closer to a deal.
Russia demands more territory in eastern Ukraine and sweeping military and political restrictions on Kyiv.
Ukraine and its allies say ceding ground to Moscow would be tantamount to a capitulation and leave Kyiv vulnerable to future Russian attacks.

articles.title: Turkey and Israel's growing rivalry in the Horn of Africa
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Turkey and Israel's growing rivalry in the Horn of Africa
The Horn of Africa is where strategic maritime corridors, fragile states, and regional ambitions converge - and it is emerging as a new front in Middle Eastern geopolitical competition.
Israel’s 26 December 2025 recognition of Somaliland’s independence added new dimensions to these tensions, intersecting with Turkey’s expanding military, economic, and diplomatic footprint in Somalia and broader partnerships across the Horn of Africa.
From Turkey’s perspective, Israel’s Somaliland move and its broader regional engagement challenge Ankara’s strategic interests. Tel Aviv, for its part, views Somaliland as a potential gateway to projecting influence near Houthi-controlled territory in Yemen and along one of the world’s most important maritime corridors.
Somaliland’s longstanding quest for international recognition risks becoming further entangled in the rivalries of Middle Eastern powers, transforming a local sovereignty dispute into a wider contest over the future of Red Sea security.
As Turkey and Israel deepen their engagement, and other external actors pursue their own agendas, the Horn of Africa might end up an increasingly crowded arena of geopolitical competition. The implications for regional stability could be serious.
Israel's Somaliland gambit and the rivalry with Turkey
Situated alongside busy maritime routes, the Horn of Africa links the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden and the Indian Ocean, occupying a position of much geostrategic importance.
Egypt, Iran, Israel, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, Turkey, and the United Arab Emirates (UAE) increasingly view the Red Sea, the Gulf of Aden, and the surrounding territories as a single security environment. Instability in one part of this interconnected region can disrupt commercial shipping, threaten energy security, and intensify rivalries among states far beyond its shores.
Israel’s decision to recognise Somaliland’s independence and to invest in deeper ties with the self-declared breakaway republic is very much about securing a strong position in a territory situated in close proximity to Yemen.
This land can provide Tel Aviv with the means to closely monitor Houthi activity, improve intelligence collection, and strengthen surveillance of maritime routes that have become increasingly vulnerable to disruption.
“Israel’s interest in the Horn of Africa is not new but has sped up amid regional shake-up in the aftermath of [7 October 2023],” Dr Burcu Ozcelik, Senior Research Fellow for Middle East Security at the London-based Royal United Services Institute (RUSI), told The New Arab.
“Israel sees Somaliland mainly through a defence cooperation lens, and as a possible staging ground for future offensive military activity against the Houthis. The strategic value of access near Yemen for Israel spans intelligence, surveillance, and potentially military operations,” she added.
Ankara and Tel Aviv’s rivalry and maritime security interests are “mutually reinforcing” motivations, argued Cameron Hudson, an independent analyst with expertise on African peace, security, and governance, who previously worked on Africa at the Central Intelligence Agency, State Department, and the US National Security Council.
“They are two sides of the same coin and cannot be disaggregated,” he told The New Arab.
However, Omar S. Mahmood, a Senior Analyst for Somalia and the Horn of Africa at International Crisis Group, offers a more qualified interpretation. He suggests that the immediate motivation for Tel Aviv is mostly related to security, while competition with Ankara is a secondary consequence, not necessarily the driving force.
“I don’t think Israel’s relationship with Somaliland is driven by a broader rivalry with Turkey per se. But there are local ramifications as Somaliland itself is seeking external allies as it is uncomfortable with growing Turkish military support to Somalia, viewing it as a potential future threat,” explained Mahmood in an interview with The New Arab.
“So, in this sense the middle powers can get drawn into supporting opposite sides in local rivalries, even if that was not the primary factor driving their engagement in the first place,” he added.
Turkey's foothold in Somalia
Turkey’s presence in Somalia is a product of many years of sustained investment and political commitment.
In 2011, Somalia faced a devastating famine which claimed approximately 250,000 lives (half of them children) amid an unprecedented humanitarian crisis. At that time, Mogadishu did not have many reliable partners around the world.
That was when Ankara’s engagement with the country gained momentum, beginning with humanitarian assistance and reconstruction before developing into a much wider relationship across multiple domains, from investment to military training and security cooperation to state-building.
Central to Turkey’s military partnership with Somalia has been its TURKSOM facility in Mogadishu. This training establishment has been at the heart of Turkish efforts to help build up the Somali government’s ability to fight al-Shabaab.
Ankara and Mogadishu signed a 10-year defence agreement in 2024, extending their cooperation into naval development and the protection of Somalia's coastline, alongside growing Turkish interests in maritime security and offshore oil and gas exploration, underscoring Turkey’s stakes in Somalia achieving greater stability.
Bilateral ties also strengthened when Somalia sought international support following Ethiopia's agreement with Somaliland concerning access to the sea in exchange for recognition - a deal which infuriated officials in Mogadishu.
Ankara subsequently helped mediate between Somalia and Ethiopia, illustrating how Turkey’s influence has gone beyond military and economic cooperation and entailed effective regional diplomacy.
In late 2025, Turkey joined many other countries around the world in strongly denouncing Israel’s recognition of Somaliland. Ankara feared that recognition of the breakaway republic gravely threatened Somalia’s territorial dignity.
Turkey also has concerns about the potential creation of openings for external actors to establish a presence for themselves in territories situated near maritime routes where Ankara has vested interests.
Rather than reacting with an immediate escalation of its military presence, Ankara seems to find its most effective response to be based on reinforcing its relationships and institutions that serve to underpin Turkish influence in Somalia. This measured approach appears to be aimed at protecting the investments which Turkey has made in the country without setting Ankara up for any overt confrontation with the Israelis in Somalia.
However, Ankara’s efforts to preserve its position in Somalia could have unintended consequences. Somaliland may interpret deeper Turkish-Somali security cooperation as a threat to its political ambitions, prompting Hargeisa to seek stronger external backing and, in the process, potentially deepening regional tensions.
The Emirati factor
No analysis of Turkish-Israeli competition in the Horn of Africa is complete without taking stock of the UAE’s role. Abu Dhabi’s support for Somaliland, even if short of formal recognition, places the UAE broadly on the same side of this sovereign dispute as Tel Aviv.
The UAE has vast strategic and commercial interests across the Red Sea, giving Abu Dhabi high stakes in the Horn of Africa’s evolving security order, while its normalised relationship with Israel continues to be an important feature of the Middle East’s geopolitical landscape more than six years after the Abraham Accords’ signing.
On the other side, Turkey, Saudi Arabia, Egypt, Qatar, and other regional actors have expressed support for Somalia’s territorial integrity, a position that connects their interests in the Horn of Africa to their wider security cooperation in the Middle East.
Hudson sees the UAE and Israel as a “powerful and mutually reinforcing duo in the Red Sea” which are both willing to challenge established power structures and intervene in disputes in the Horn of Africa to further their national interests at the region’s expense.
“They are happy to pick winners and losers, unsettle established power dynamics, and actively intervene in regional politics and conflicts in ways that benefit them even if that means unsettling regional dynamics,” he told The New Arab.
Hudson contrasts this with “Turkish or Saudi efforts to stabilise and reinforce established power dynamics as a way of limiting destabilising outside influences.”
Clearly, Abu Dhabi’s role is important not only due to Emirati ambitions but also because external backing can make local leaders less willing to compromise by reducing the perceived costs associated with confrontation.
The local stakes of a wider geopolitical contest
Despite the growing involvement of Middle Eastern states in the Horn of Africa, and the risks of this region becoming more of an arena for external competition, it is necessary to note that Somalia and Somaliland are not passive actors victimised by a giant game of geopolitical chess.
Both have agency and are actively seeking non-African partners to strengthen their positions and advance their political objectives.
For the government in Mogadishu, Turkey's military, economic, and diplomatic support is critical to strengthening state institutions, improving security, and protecting Somalia’s territorial integrity.
Meanwhile, Somaliland has long sought international recognition and has strong incentives to cultivate relationships with countries such as Israel and the UAE, which might advance that goal or at least provide greater protection against perceived threats.
In this sense, “you have a layer of local rivalries that now intersect with regional rivalries, creating a potentially dangerous situation,” explained Mahmood, who emphasised that this permits “Horn of Africa actors to take on more maximalist, aggressive and less compromising positions, knowing that [they] have…external support to fall back on.”
Houthi missile and drone attacks on Saudi Arabia, Israel, and maritime targets have done much to help explain why regional powers see the Horn of Africa as increasingly important to their foreign policy calculations.
As Houthi-Saudi hostilities escalate, Riyadh is focused on growing stronger security partnerships with regional actors, while governments in the Horn of Africa are likely to view closer cooperation with the Kingdom as a way to secure higher levels of assistance and bolster their own military capabilities. Meanwhile, the conflict in Sudan adds new layers of complication as it draws regional actors into overlapping security and political calculations.
Yet a greater military presence does not necessarily translate into greater stability. While competing powers expand their security footholds with the aim of countering one another, mistrust can deepen, territorial disputes can intensify, and local actors will probably pursue greater support from external powers.
Therefore, the Horn of Africa is increasingly likely to become exposed to conflicts in and around the Red Sea even if not directly involved in their initial escalation. Within this context, heightened insecurity means that further militarisation of the Red Sea risks undermining, rather than enhancing, security.
An evolving security arrangement around the Red Sea
On 7 August, Turkey, Saudi Arabia, and Pakistan signed the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement - a trilateral alliance which is defensive in nature and aimed at containing the chaotic instability unleashed by the war centred on Iran.
This security configuration has potentially significant implications for the balance of power around the Red Sea and Horn of Africa. It was hardly surprising that the leadership in Mogadishu hailed the pact in the immediate aftermath of its announcement, especially given Somalia’s close ties with the three signatories and shared threat perceptions of Israeli aggression.
For Somalia, the pact’s significance extends beyond its endorsement and raises important questions about regional realignments and Ankara’s position in the Horn of Africa within the wider context of an emerging security architecture.
Escalating Houthi-Saudi hostilities prompt a broader recalibration of regional security alignments, bringing Turkey and Pakistan closer to Saudi Arabia through the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement. For Ankara, this partnership offers an opportunity to connect its longstanding presence in Somalia with a wider strategic role in Gulf and Red Sea security.
Dr Ozcelik told The New Arab that the hostilities have “crossed red lines that were deemed unthinkable not long ago,” setting in motion a realignment among Riyadh’s allies. Ankara’s growing institutional engagement with the Kingdom therefore extends beyond diplomatic rhetoric, highlighting a more formal commitment to regional defence and security cooperation.
There are implications of this emerging Turkish-Saudi alignment for the rivalry between Ankara and Tel Aviv. As Dr Ozcelik stressed, Ankara is “institutionalising its partnership with Saudi Arabia beyond rhetoric and through defence commitments, minilateralism, and regional diplomacy.”
This closer Turkish-Saudi relationship will not escape Israeli strategists’ attention, particularly as Ankara expands its regional security role while Riyadh remains firm in its support for Palestinian statehood.
In Dr Ozcelik’s assessment, these parallel developments risk “fuelling a greater gulf between Israel and Turkey,” further complicating an already tense relationship that has significantly deteriorated since 7 October 2023.
While commentators sometimes toss Somalia around as a possible Mecca Joint Defence Agreement candidate, Hudson considers formal Somalia membership in the pact unlikely in the near term. He noted that Somalia remains a recipient of security assistance rather than a country capable of contributing meaningfully to a mutual defence arrangement.
“Given the high level of instability still emanating from Somalia, external countries would be foolish at this point to enter into a mutual security agreement with them now. Somalia can’t provide for its own security, let alone contribute to the security of others,” Hudson told The New Arab.
Similarly, Mahmood does not expect Somalia to formally join the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement. But he does think Mogadishu is likely to deepen security relations with the pact’s three signatories, noting that this is a development already underway. “Somalia prefers to align with this bloc of countries and sees them as a future source of support as it continues to build up its military capabilities,” he observed.
The risks of an expanding geopolitical contest
The internationalisation of the Horn of Africa’s political disputes and security crises entered a new chapter after Israel became the first UN member-state to officially recognise Somaliland ten months ago.
What started as a dispute over Somaliland’s recognition and Somalia’s territorial integrity has transformed into a larger contest over maritime security, military access, and regional influence.
A dangerous risk is an exacerbating security dilemma in which competing alliances deepen mistrust, undermine compromise, and expose the Horn of Africa to conflicts originating elsewhere.
Preventing further escalation will require Middle Eastern powers and their regional partners to exercise restraint while recognising that lasting stability depends on addressing the disputes that drive Somalia and Somaliland to seek competing external allies.

articles.title: Ukraine war briefing: Outrage in Europe after Russian drone kills 14 on rail platform in Dnipro
articles.body:
- European leaders have reacted with outrage to a deadly attack by a Russian drone that slammed into a busy railway platform in the Ukrainian city of Dnipro on Thursday, as Volodymyr Zelenskyy warned Ukraine had intelligence about more ballistic missile strikes to come. French President Emmanuel Macron stressed the need for “far more than a localised ceasefire”, referencing the current truce in the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky. The EU council president, António Costa, who described the Dnipro attacks as “cruel and devastating”, called for greater pressure on Russia after the latest strikes against civilians. “The EU will continue to increase the pressure on Russia and to support Ukraine until a just and lasting peace is achieved,” he added. “We call on all our international partners to do the same.”
- Later on Thursday, Russian forces launched an attack on the Ukrainian capital Kyiv with ballistic missiles, Mayor Vitali Klitschko said on Telegram, hitting warehouses and triggering a fire. Emergency services were headed to the scene on the east side of the Dnipro River, he said.
- Describing the Dnipro train station attack – which killed at least 14 people and injured another 14 – as “horrific”, the president of Ukraine insisted “sanctions against Moscow and its war machine must not be eased for as long as this Russian war continues”. Zelenskyy warned also that Ukraine had intelligence about preparations by the Russians of new ballistic missile strikes. “We need the means to take out all this Russian evil. We are expecting relevant decisions,” he said. Another attack on Dnipro hit a student dormitory, setting it ablaze, regional governor Oleksandr Hanzha said, adding the assaults had cut power to 350,000 households.
- The strikes came as Ukraine and Russia kept to a fragile local ceasefire in the ravaged city of Oleshky – under Russian occupation since 2022 and where residents have faced months of food, water and medicine shortages. While the truce held into a third day, strikes elsewhere in Ukraine killed at least 20 people and injured more than 70 people, according to local officials. Russia and Ukraine said on Thursday an operation to bring aid into the town and allow residents to leave was ready to begin.
- Meanwhile, Ukraine’s military has paused its strikes on Russian oil refineries after pressure from US President Donald Trump, according to a report in the Wall Street Journal on Thursday, citing people with knowledge of the operations. Ukrainian units carrying out long-range strikes were told in mid-October that the campaign against refineries was effectively on hold once missions already in motion were completed, the Journal reported. The unofficial pause is expected to last until after the US midterm elections and potentially deeper into November, the newspaper said.
- After the Dnipro attack, Zelenskyy renewed his criticism of a deal struck between Trump and Russia’s President Vladimir Putin to ease some US sanctions on Russia allowing Moscow to release diesel on to global markets. “How many such terrorist strikes has Russia carried out against our people since sanctions were lifted on some Russian oligarchs and the energy sector, instead of de-escalating?” he asked.
- Late on Thursday, Putin said he supported any steps aimed at restoring relations with European countries, saying the outbreak of any conflict would leave a situation with no winners. Commenting on his phone call this week with the leaders of Norway and Finland, Putin told reporters after hosting a summit with African leaders: “And if anyone wants it, let them prepare, but right now they have not achieved their goal – to inflict a strategic defeat on Russia. And if things go too far, there will be no winners at all. .”
