articles.title: Putin Says Nordic Leaders Were Right to Call Him, Despite EU Criticism
articles.body:
Russian President Vladimir Putin defended Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre over their Oct. 27 telephone call with him, saying they were right to reach out despite criticism from other European leaders.
Speaking at a press conference after the Russia-Africa summit on Thursday, Oct. 29, Putin confirmed that the conversation took place at the initiative of the Nordic leaders and covered a wide range of issues.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“I know that criticism was later directed at them, but it is not for us to judge whether this [the call] is right or wrong. I believe it is right,” Putin said, according to Interfax-Ru.
“After all, there are people in Europe who do not want to inflict a strategic defeat on Russia, as some do, but want to establish some kind of constructive dialogue,” he added.
The remarks came on the same day that the Kremlin ruled out European participation in the next month’s Abu Dhabi negotiations with Ukraine and the US.
Dialogue offer paired with a warning
Moscow, according to the Russian president, backs any effort to rebuild relations with Europe, whether with the EU as a bloc or individual countries.
Russia has always supported steps toward restoring “full-format and full-fledged relations” with European states, he added.
However, during the same remarks, Putin warned that a war between Russia and Europe would have “no winners,” claiming that the West had failed in its goal of inflicting a strategic defeat on Russia and was unlikely to achieve it by 2030, Russian-state owned media TASS reported.
Ukraine's Neptune Missiles Destroy 2 Russian Su-34 Bombers in Volgograd Region
The warning comes as European governments step up preparations for a possible confrontation.
Germany’s elite KSK special forces began training for a role in conventional warfare with Russia, shifting away from its traditional focus on hostage rescue and counterterrorism, Brig. Gen. Andreas Kuhne told Germany’s BILD earlier this week.
European countries are also facing a rise in hybrid warfare threats, including sabotage, espionage, cyberattacks and frequent drone incursions into their airspace.
While some European leaders have described the situation as already amounting to a war, as the line between hybrid tactics and direct conflict continues to blur, others have been more cautious, refraining from such labels to avoid escalating tensions with Moscow.
Mixed reaction from European leaders
The abrupt discussion drew a mixed response from Ukraine’s European allies, particularly from other Nordic countries, who said the call was not coordinated with them in advance.
Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said she was “very sceptical about this independent initiative by Norway and Finland,” Euronews reported, adding that Russia’s ongoing escalation against Ukraine remains evidence that “Moscow is not serious about diplomacy.”
“We have previously emphasised, with clear backing from the rest of Europe, that when others have gone solo and, for example, travelled to Moscow, it is crucial that we, Europeans, stand together,” she continued, in a reference to former Hungary Prime Minister Viktor Orbán who flew to Russia to meet with Putin at the time of his tenure.
Swedish Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson reiterated that she also has “pretty low expectations for this kind of [direct] talk.”
Støre defended the call by saying Europe needs to speak with Russia, instead of only relying on messages mediated by the US administration, which has a different take on the war.
The content of the call had also become a point of dispute.
On Wednesday, Oct. 28, the Financial Times reported that Putin spent much of their 90-minute conversation discussing medieval history, while an immediate ceasefire was barely raised.
Støre rejected the FT’s report, asking the newspaper to correct it. “That he gave a lecture on Slavic history is simply not correct,” he said, adding that the time was distributed relatively evenly between the participants. The newspaper has refused to issue a correction.
The call came after a week of diplomacy involving the two Nordic leaders.
On Oct. 20, they hosted a meeting between President Volodymyr Zelensky and senior US envoy Steve Witkoff for talks in Oslo, with US President Donald Trump’s son-in-law, Jared Kushner, joining remotely.
Witkoff then traveled to St. Petersburg for a direct meeting with Putin on Oct. 21, where he urged Putin to consider resuming trilateral talks with Ukraine and the US, bringing documents outlining approaches to ending the war.
The Kremlin reiterated that a just and lasting peace in Ukraine was possible only if Russia’s interests were taken into account.

articles.title: Six lanes and metro line under fire: Kyiv prepares about $22 million for backup river crossings after Russian strike on Southern Bridge
articles.body:
The Ukrainian government has instructed Kyiv to establish alternative routes after Russian attacks stopped traffic on one of the capital’s main bridges. The city authorities will bear the cost of the new crossings, with Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko saying the city needs an additional $22 million.
This year, Russia has launched tactics to spread panic among civilians and trigger more people to leave the country. In the latest attack, several Russia's ballistic missiles struck the Southern Bridge, used for vehicle and metro traffic, breaking a huge hole and paralyzing all the pathes. The bridge was closed. Now, there is a fear that more bridges can be targeted this way, dividing Kyiv in two parts.
The situation is urgent, as Ukrainian Transport Minister Mykola Kalashnyk says about 600,000 vehicles cross the Dnipro in Kyiv every day.
What is Kyiv’s response to the winter terror?
According to Klitschko, Kyiv convened the capital’s Defense Council on 28 October to find an answer to this difficult question.
The agenda included implementing a project to build combined water crossings over the Dnipro River and access roads to them.
“The military command will determine the locations, with approval to be granted, among others, by the Kyiv City Military Administration,” Klitschko said.
Under the government’s recommendations, the Kyiv city authorities must find $22 million for the project.
Klitschko had previously faced heavy criticism after it emerged that the city lacked sufficient shelters and last winter exposed serious shortcomings in preparing infrastructure for Russian attacks. These included a lack of alternative energy supply routes, poorly distributed energy, burst heating pipes that flooded apartments, and the inability of people with disabilities to reach shelters without elevators.
The mayor himself said the problems stemmed from the central government withholding funding, which had stalled numerous energy resilience projects and delayed their implementation.
The latest announcement also indicates that Kyiv has once again taken on the financial burden itself.
Meanwhile, Ukraine has been working with Japan on backup crossings. Tokyo has already delivered 720 meters of prefabricated bridge structures to Ukraine. The two sides are currently exploring how this equipment could be used to establish alternative crossings.
Step two: strengthening existing infrastructure
Another option is to reinforce existing bridges. City specialists are developing additional technical solutions to protect bridges across the Dnipro River, Klitschko said in his statement on 27 October, adding that proposals from the military had also been heard.
The issue of installing mobile shelters was also raised on the same day, the mayor of Kyiv said in a separate statement on his Telegram channel on 27 October. Despite intensifying Russian attacks and about, as Radio Svoboda reported in its article on 30 September, $11 million set aside in 2025, Kyiv still has only a handful of mobile shelters: LB reported in December 2025 that district tenders failed. Donors paid for the first one at a bus stop, the Kyiv City State Administration said on 15 October.
Klitschko raised the issue of shelters again after a court on 12 October ruled that local authorities must urgently install mobile shelters in public areas, including near public transport stops, parks, and squares, according to Kyiv’s Prosecutor’s Office.
Russia hits the Southern Bridge again
On 2 October, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in an interview with the Financial Times that Russian ruler Vladimir Putin had ordered the lifting of previous restrictions on airstrikes. Among new targets, according to him, were bridges, data centers, internet, mobile networks, hospitals, kindergartens, schools, and universities.
The night of 26–27 October showed what that looks like. Russia launched ballistic missile attacks in a few waves, and the second of them hit the Southern Bridge and the metro infrastructure on it, Klitschko said. The structure carries six lanes of road traffic and two metro tracks.
Zelenskyy put the night’s total at 16 ballistic missiles and blamed delays in deliveries of Patriot and NASAMS interceptors: “Every such delay is a new Russian hit on one target or another.”

articles.title: Investing in conventional weapons better than developing nuclear program of one's own – expert
articles.body:
Investing in conventional weapons better than developing nuclear program of one's own – expert
Jim Stokes, a GLOBSEC expert and former NATO Director of Nuclear Policy (2023-2025), expressed this view in an interview with Ukrinform.
"Ukraine joining NATO. That is the most credible option. NATO's deterrence has worked for more than 77 years because no state has ever attacked the Alliance. I do not usually use the word 'guarantee,' but there are benefits to being covered by extended nuclear deterrence from the United States, the United Kingdom and France," the expert said.
At the same time, he cautioned against expecting a nuclear program of one's own to provide absolute protection. Stokes, who headed the Staff Group of NATO's Nuclear Planning Group, outlined his arguments.
According to him, the decision to develop an independent nuclear capability cannot be taken lightly, as no one wants further proliferation of nuclear weapons, which are currently possessed by only a limited number of states. Political commitments, financial costs, the technical expertise and technology required, and the time and money needed to produce a certain number of nuclear weapons must all be taken into account. In addition, a country would need delivery systems, a doctrine, command-and-control procedures, and many other supporting capabilities.
"All of this requires a great deal of effort. I say this as someone who worked for a long time on countering the proliferation of weapons of mass destruction," Stokes said.
He also cited North Korea as an example of a country that has become a nuclear power. However, the expert noted, North Korea is a pariah state. Ukraine, or any other country, therefore needs to consider whether it wants to become a pariah and potentially face sanctions by withdrawing from the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons. "Would that really provide the security they seek?" he said.
At the same time, Stokes acknowledged that he understood those who argue that, from a national security perspective, nuclear weapons offer the ultimate guarantee of national security and sovereignty.
The expert therefore believes it would be better to devote time, money and effort to conventional defense.
"Whether you can be part of a nuclear alliance and reinforce that arrangement, as in NATO or another alliance, or whether there are other ways to obtain some form of security guarantee. There seem to be better options that would be available rather than pursuing a national nuclear weapons program," Stokes concluded.
As Ukrinform reported, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said that in exchange for giving up its nuclear weapons, Ukraine should have received a "security umbrella." He described the guarantees the country received at the time as "an unfair game and a major mistake."

articles.title: Polish defence ministry confirms transfer of two MiG-29 jets to Ukraine
articles.body:
Polish defence ministry confirms transfer of two MiG-29 jets to Ukraine
Polish Defence Ministry representative Dariusz Łukowski has said that Poland will send two MiG-29 fighter jets to Ukraine in the near future.
Source: Polish media outlet Rzeczpospolita, citing the Director of the Strategy and Defence Planning Department of the Ministry of National Defence of Poland, as reported by European Pravda
Details: Rzeczpospolita reported that Poland will transfer two MiG-29 aircraft to Ukraine as part of its latest assistance package worth approximately €50 million.
In addition to the fighter jets, the country will also provide ammunition.
Łukowski also confirmed the transfer of two fighter jets to Ukraine. When asked when the transfer would take place, he replied: "In the near future. The decision has been made, and these two MiG-29s will be transferred."
It is reported that one of the aircraft has already reached the end of its service life, while the second is still airworthy.
Rzeczpospolita also noted that the aid package will include 155mm and 152mm artillery ammunition, 20 by 102mm ammunition for the six-barrelled cannons on F-16 fighter jets, as well as missiles for Piorun man-portable air defence systems.
Quote from the Polish Ministry of National Defence: "Poland is preparing another aid package for Ukraine. The scope of this support is determined by safety considerations for the Polish state and the resources of the armed forces, as established by the chief of the General Staff. As stated by the minister of national defence, we are preparing aid that includes equipment that the Polish Armed Forces are decommissioning (as it has reached the end of its service life) – equipment that will no longer be used by the Polish military, but may still be useful in Ukraine."
Meanwhile, the ministry declined to provide detailed information regarding what else will be included in the aid package for Ukraine due to confidentiality.
Background:
- In August, Ukraine's Ambassador to Poland Vasyl Bodnar said that dialogue with Poland on the transfer of four MiG-29 fighter jets was continuing, but there were several obstacles.
- In late June, Polish Defence Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz had said Ukraine had withdrawn from the proposed "MiGs for drones" agreement. A few days later, he claimed the decision had been driven by the historical dispute between Kyiv and Warsaw.
- However, in July, Kosiniak-Kamysz spoke of progress in implementing the agreement.
- He later stated that Bulgaria wished to buy the Polish MiG-29 jets in which Ukraine was interested, but Warsaw was still not ruling out attempts to reach an agreement with Kyiv.

articles.title: Ukraine’s Linza bomber drone clears path for UGV in German exercise
articles.body:
- Frontline Robotics’ Linza drone took part in Quantum Systems’ Forward Edge 26 exercise in Germany, working with other unmanned systems through MOSAIC UXS.
- In one scenario, a Vector drone spotted simulated enemy drones on a ground vehicle’s route and Linza struck them with payload drops.
Ukrainian drone maker Frontline Robotics flew its Linza bomber drone alongside German, Ukrainian and other unmanned air, ground and sea systems during Forward Edge 26, a two-week exercise in Germany hosted by Quantum Systems, the company said on social media.
In one deployment, Quantum Systems’ Vector reconnaissance drone spotted simulated enemy drones along the route of an unmanned ground vehicle, and Linza then attacked the targets by dropping payloads, clearing the way for the ground vehicle, Frontline Robotics said. The company said the drone completed its missions in heavy rain and dense fog, but it did not say how many sorties it flew or how many targets it hit.
All of the systems in the exercise were connected through MOSAIC UXS, Quantum Systems’ software for controlling and coordinating unmanned platforms from different manufacturers in a single operational picture. Quantum Systems said it ran Forward Edge 26 at a military training area in central Germany and wrapped it up on Oct. 22, with no crewed vehicles in the scenarios. Systems located in Ukraine, the United States and Australia were also flown remotely during the event.
The exercise was built around four scenarios: defense against an attacking force, convoy and force protection, coastal and port surveillance, and minelaying and route clearance. In the convoy scenario, laser-based counter-drone systems protected an unmanned convoy, while the maritime scenario linked aerial and sea-based systems for coastal monitoring. Industry participants included Daimler Truck, Volkswagen, XTEND, Planet and Quantum Systems’ German-Ukrainian joint ventures, Quantum Frontline Industries and Quantum Tencore Industries.
Linza, which means “lens” in Ukrainian, is a quadcopter that can drop munitions on targets, lay mines, carry a radio relay, scout and deliver small loads of supplies to frontline positions. Frontline Robotics first introduced it in 2024 and unveiled the Linza 3.0 version in February, which the company says carries up to 4 kg (8.8 pounds) over a tactical range of 15 km (9 miles), with AI-assisted visual navigation that lets it hold position over a target without relying on satellite signals. Frontline Robotics says more than 80 units of Ukraine’s Defense Forces now use the drone.
Quantum Systems and Frontline Robotics build Linza together through Quantum Frontline Industries, a joint venture whose factory outside Munich opened in February in the presence of German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and is meant to eventually produce more than 10,000 drones a year. Germany has funded joint production of the Linza under the Build with Ukraine program, and earlier this month the joint venture signed a contract to supply Linza and Zoom reconnaissance drones to Ukraine’s National Guard in 2027.
Quantum Systems’ own Vector, the reconnaissance drone that cued Linza’s strike in the exercise, has flown extensively in Ukraine, including a mission in which one aircraft survived 11 hits and kept flying. Frontline Robotics also builds the Burya remote weapon turret, which Danish company Dropla has agreed to integrate on its unmanned ground vehicles.

articles.title: Saudi-led coalition says intercepted Houthi missiles; Houthis claim 27 killed in Saudi airstrikes
articles.body:
SANAA/RIYADH, Oct. 29 (Xinhua) -- Saudi air defenses intercepted and destroyed two ballistic missiles launched by Yemen's Houthi group toward the Saudi capital Riyadh, the Saudi-led coalition said on Thursday evening, while the Houthis said 27 people were killed in Saudi airstrikes on Houthi-held areas in Yemen.
Loud explosions were heard in Riyadh earlier in the day. Local residents received alerts via mobile apps.
In a separate statement on Thursday morning, the coalition said Saudi air defenses intercepted and destroyed a Houthi ballistic missile launched toward the kingdom's Eastern Province.
Meanwhile, the Houthi group said through its al-Masirah TV channel that 27 people, including women and children, were killed and 18 others wounded in airstrikes in the northern province of Al-Jawf and the southwestern province of Taiz within less than 24 hours.
In a statement, Houthi military spokesman Yahya Sarea said Saudi forces carried out 116 air and missile strikes over the past 24 hours across Houthi-held areas in six Yemeni provinces.
The figures could not be independently verified.
Also on Thursday, Majid al-Nuzaili, spokesperson for Yemen's government forces, said the forces conducted 982 attacks over the past 24 hours using warplanes, drones, artillery and rocket launchers against the Houthis.
Al-Nuzaili said the attacks targeted Houthi reinforcements, command centers, firing positions and supply lines, claiming that 324 Houthi fighters and commanders were "neutralized" and 108 military vehicles and weapons were destroyed or damaged.
The developments came amid escalating hostilities between the Houthis and Saudi Arabia, with the two sides exchanging cross-border strikes in recent weeks.
Yemen has been mired in conflict since late 2014, when the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa and much of northern Yemen, prompting the Saudi-led coalition to intervene in 2015 in support of the Yemeni government. ■

articles.title: Putin says Russia is ready for war with Europe
articles.body:
- Vladimir Putin said on Oct. 29 that Russia is ready for war with Europe but does not want one, warning there would be no winners.
- He spoke in Moscow after the Russia-Africa summit, responding to European plans to be ready to repel a Russian attack by 2030.
Russian President Vladimir Putin said on Oct. 29 that Russia is “ready” for a war with Europe but does not want one, and warned that a conflict between them would leave no winners, responding to European warnings that Moscow could be able to attack NATO by the end of the decade.
Putin made the remarks at a press conference in Moscow after the Russia-Africa summit, held jointly with the African Union’s chairman, Burundian President Évariste Ndayishimiye, The Moscow Times reported, citing Interfax. He was asked about his recent phone calls with Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre, and said Russia supports any steps to restore full relations with European countries, either with the European Union as a whole or one by one.
“Many are talking about preparing for war by 2030. First of all, we are ready, but we do not want any war with Europe. If they want to prepare, let them prepare,” said Putin.
He added that Europe had not managed to inflict a “strategic defeat” on Russia and was unlikely to do so by 2030, according to TV Rain.
“If things go too far, there will be no winners at all. Let no one forget that,” Putin said.
Putin also referred to tensions in the Baltic Sea, asking whether anyone wanted the region to end up like the Persian Gulf or the Strait of Hormuz, and said Russia did not want that but would respond to any challenge. He did not name any country or describe what kind of response he meant.
The 2030 date Putin cited matches the timeline European governments have set for rearmament. EU states aim to be able to repel a Russian attack by 2030, and several European officials have warned that Russia could rebuild enough military strength to strike a NATO member before then. German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius and the head of Germany’s armed forces, Gen. Carsten Breuer, have said Russia could be capable of a large-scale conventional attack on NATO territory by 2029, and a classified German intelligence and military analysis reported in 2025 said Moscow was preparing the conditions for a conventional war against NATO, with the Baltic states a possible target. Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk has said Europe should be prepared for a possible major conflict with Russia as early as 2027.
The Kremlin has repeatedly rejected those warnings, and Putin has long said Russia has no plans to attack NATO countries. In December 2025, he said that if Europe “suddenly wants to wage a war with us and starts it, we are ready right away,” Fox News reported, while also saying Moscow did not seek war with Europe. European leaders, for their part, say Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, now in its fifth year, shows why they need to rearm.
Putin’s latest comments came two days after his calls with Stubb and Støre, which European officials have not described in detail. Neither Finland nor Norway, both NATO members that border Russia, had publicly responded to Putin’s remarks by Thursday evening.

articles.title: NATO–Ukraine AI Forecasts Russian Drone Threats 24 Hours Ahead, 50 Kilometers Behind Front
articles.body:
- Category
- War in Ukraine
NATO–Ukraine AI Forecasts Russian Drone Threats 24 Hours Ahead, 50 Kilometers Behind Front
NATO and Ukraine have developed an artificial intelligence system capable of predicting Russian drone activity up to 24 hours in advance across areas extending 50 kilometers behind the front line, Business Insider reported on October 29.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The system, known as Initiative 13 or Model 13, generates predictive maps to help Ukrainian commanders anticipate Russian drone operations and position troops and equipment. A spokesperson for NATO’s Joint Analysis, Training, and Education Center (JATEC) explained that the technology "turns an array of disparate data into a clear map of expected activity."
Initiative 13 covers Ukrainian territory between 5 and 50 kilometers behind the line of contact, dividing the area into geographical cells. For each cell, the system forecasts the intensity of Russian reconnaissance and strike drone activity, threat levels, potential changes, and possible variations in drone operations.
The AI analyzes historical battlefield data, including previous Russian drone activity, aircraft types, deployment patterns, weather conditions, terrain, and proximity to the front line. Its forecasts identify high-risk areas for the following day, allowing commanders to adjust deployments and potentially reduce exposure to Russian strikes.
However, JATEC emphasized that the system is intended to support military planning rather than replace real-time intelligence or commanders' decisions.
Ukraine's Ministry of Defense announced on October 13 that Model 13 had been validated using real-world battlefield data and was ready for integration into the Armed Forces' situational-awareness systems. The ministry described its ability to predict Russian drone operations as highly probable, although no specific accuracy figures were disclosed.
Ukrainian forces already operate the Delta battlefield management platform, which consolidates frontline intelligence into an interactive map accessible through computers, tablets, and smartphones. Model 13 was developed jointly by Ukraine's Armed Forces and NATO's Allied Command Transformation, with support from JATEC.
The push toward data-driven warfare is also reshaping how Ukrainian units record and reuse combat results. Between March and October 1, drone operators logged more than 3 million strike missions through Mission Control, a Delta module that feeds completed mission data back into future planning.
In September alone, troops entered more than 1.8 million mission results, a more than ninefold increase over monthly usage at the start of 2026. By July, the system was already recording more than 6,600 confirmed enemy targets hit each day.

articles.title: Von der Leyen’s Canada power play: Words fail the EU boss
articles.body:
Von der Leyen’s Canada power play: Words fail the EU boss
EU Commission President Ursula von der Leyen is stirring up trouble at home during a controversial trip to Montreal, turning what should have been a straightforward trade mission into a petty argument over Canada’s fictional “membership” in the bloc.
The EU mandarin traveled to Montreal for the 21st annual EU-Canada summit on Thursday, with her tail between her legs. A month after unilaterally promising Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney “associate member” status of the bloc, she was reportedly forced to scrub all mentions of the term and downgrade her offer to one of an “ever closer association” between the EU and Canada.
When the summit closes on Friday, both sides will issue a revised joint statement that reads: “We will create an even closer association between Canada and the EU... and work to define by the 2027 EU-Canada Summit the concept of an ever closer association of Canada to the EU, short of full membership itself,” according to a draft seen by Policito.
Why was the text changed?
Von der Leyen reportedly gave neither the EU’s vast bureaucracy, nor its members’ wary leaders, any warning before she told Carney in front of the European Parliament that she “would like to work with you on opening the door for Canada to being the first associate member of the European Union.”
Unilateral decisions and boundary-overstepping are von der Leyen’s calling cards, as her fellow Eurocrats have repeatedly complained to the press. “Nobody was consulted about associate membership apart from [von der Leyen’s] closest staff, it would seem,” an unnamed diplomat told The Guardian on Wednesday. The widespread anonymous briefing to various mainstream European media made it clear that France, Germany, Greece and Italy had forced von der Leyen to adopt the new, watered-down terminology.
Ursula goes rogue
In her first speech in Montreal on Thursday, von der Leyen refused to adopt the new, sanitized wording. After noting that “Canada cannot become a full-fledged member of the EU because of geography,” she insisted that “we are discussing the idea of Canada becoming the first associate member of the European Union. Our idea is simple: it is an ‘association without accession’.”
Whatever form Friday’s communique will take, von der Leyen has evidently chosen to disregard the concerns of the EU’s largest member states for the sake of her own personal project. However, the difference between both statements is purely rhetorical.
What does ‘associate member’ mean anyway?
Neither “Associate member” nor “ever closer association” are defined anywhere in EU law.
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz attempted to define “associate membership” in May when he suggested that it be granted to Ukraine. Under his proposal, Ukraine would participate in European Council meetings without voting rights, send representatives to the European Parliament, receive more EU funding, and become party to the EU’s mutual defense clause.
The proposal was rejected by Kiev, with Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky arguing that this kind of ‘membership-lite’ would leave his country “present in the European Union, but voiceless.”
“Ever closer association” is an even more meaningless term, lifted straight from ‘Ever Closer Union’, a hagiography on EU integration by the bloc’s court historian, Desmond Dinan. Writing in 1994, Dinan argued that “European integration is a good thing,” and the phrases he used – “ever closer union” and “pooling sovereignty,” for example – have since become staples of EU speeches and press releases.
US President Donald Trump ridiculed von der Leyen’s word games last month, calling the concept of associate membership “laughable,” and threatening to “put very serious tariffs or stop trading with Europe on many things” if the EU-Canada proto-alliance ever harmed US interests.
Carney – who plainly insisted last month that Canada is “not looking to become a member of the European Union” – responded diplomatically to the intra-EU squabbling. “The good news is it doesn’t matter about specific names or nomenclature,” he said ahead of the summit. “What matters is the difference it will make to the lives of Canadians.”
However, Von der Leyen’s “membership” promise and the subsequent retraction has undermined Carney in front of his opponents. In a social media post on Thursday, Conservative leader Pierre Poilievre described the concept of “associate membership” as “theater,” and dismissed the summit as “yet another grand theatrical meeting to sign a bunch of meaningless declarations filled with big words (catalyze, anyone?) and promises to meet again to talk more."
How long will this theatre go on? While Canadians can’t afford food and homes, Mr. Carney has distracted for months with big talk about “Associate Membership” with Europe. Now, Europe has rejected it. For the next two days, we will be distracted again from the cost-of-living crisis with wall-to-wall media coverage on yet another grand theatrical meeting to sign a bunch of meaningless declarations filled with big words (catalyze, anyone?) and promises to meet again to talk more. No one’s mortgage or grocery bill will come down. We already have a free trade deal with Europe, Mr. Carney. Get the 9 countries who have not ratified it to do so. And get EU countries to let our beef into the continent and cancel their planned carbon tariff on Canada. Otherwise stop wasting your time and our money. Both are running out.
— Pierre Poilievre (@PierrePoilievre) October 29, 2026
What does von der Leyen actually want?
Von der Leyen has far more riding on this summit than Carney. While the EU needs energy, minerals, and Canada’s geographic clout in the Arctic, Canada only needs to diversify some of its trade away from the US – which accounts for around 72% of its exports and 46% of its imports – in order to hedge against Trump’s tariffs and trade restrictions. At present, the EU accounts for less than 6% of Canada’s exports and 12% of its imports.
🛬 Touchdown in Montréal 🇨🇦 Rarely have I looked forward to a Summit this much. An ocean separates Europe and Canada. Yet we have never felt closer. We have a new ambition: bringing Canada closer to us than ever before, as Associate Member of the EU. And we want to take our unique partnership even further. With an Alliance for the Future, we will stand together and respond to a world of growing rivalries. Montréal, we’re about to write a new chapter in our shared history.
— Ursula von der Leyen (@vonderleyen) October 28, 2026
Although the agenda is wrapped up in the language of “shared values” and “respect for the rules-based international order,” Brussels’ priorities in Montreal are clear: the energy-starved EU needs access to Canada’s resources.
According to Euronews, the latest draft of the joint declaration includes a promise to “assess opportunities for long-term energy connectivity,” including the supply of Canadian liquefied natural gas to the EU. Remember that in July 2025 von der Leyen personally pledged to Trump that bloc members would buy $750 billion worth of US energy by the end of 2028, in a trade deal that was widely seen as one-sided.
Canadian Finance Minister Francois-Philippe Champagne has also announced that Ottawa and Brussels intend to sign an agreement on the supply of critical minerals including lithium, nickel, and cobalt. The EU currently controls less than 4% of the world’s supply of these minerals, which are vital in the production of electric vehicles and missiles – both of which the EU intends to increase.
The Europeans also intend to sign defense production and technology-sharing deals, to squeeze cash out of Canada for the bloc’s increasingly stretched €90 billion loan package for Ukraine, and deepen involvement in the Arctic, according to the summit agenda. As the EU set out in its updated Arctic Strategy’ earlier this month, Brussels intends to increase its military presence to challenge Russia in the north, and plans to literally redraw the map of the region to increase its meager Arctic claims, and to pursue closer ties “with like-minded partners,” including Canada.
To challenge Russia in the Arctic, the EU likely has its eyes on Canada’s polar-trained military and its 20-strong icebreaker fleet, compared to the ten such vessels spread across the 27-member bloc. None of these icebreakers are nuclear powered, and even if they were to operate on joint Arctic missions, they would be outnumbered and outclassed by Russia’s fleet of 43, eight of which are nuclear powered
However, any hope von der Leyen may have had of securing preferential single market-style trade deals with Carney have apparently been dashed. According to AFP, the “associate member” version of the joint statement included an “explicit goal of deeper financial market integration.” The new, “ever closer association” communique has replaced this with a promise by both sides to “limit potential negative effects on each other.”
Von der Leyen’s unforced error
Whether von der Leyen will, by virtue of repetition and against the will of four EU member states, invent an “associate membership” is immaterial. The concept is a legal fiction, and by insisting on the word “membership,” the European Commission president set herself up for an entirely avoidable clash with the French, Germans, Greeks, and Italians.
It’s very interesting to see the Commission president goes so defiantly against the position of Germany — the biggest member state and her home country — on an issue that, as of now, remains strictly theoretical.
— Jorge Liboreiro (@JorgeLiboreiro) October 29, 2026
The argument over the statement’s wording has overshadowed the summit, but the geopolitical reality remains unchanged: the EU needs Canada’s energy supplies to keep its economy afloat, Canada’s money to prop up its Ukraine project, and Canada’s geography to legitimize its Arctic expansion. For these, it doesn’t matter how the deal is dressed up.

articles.title: USA Delays Delivery of PAC-3 Missiles for Ukraine’s Patriot Systems but Continues to Supply PAC-2 Missiles
articles.body:
The United States is delaying the delivery of PAC-3 interceptor missiles to Ukraine for the Patriot air defense systems.
This was reported by Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty, citing an anonymous informed source within NATO.
These PAC-3 anti-aircraft missiles are primarily designed to intercept and destroy ballistic targets.
At the same time, PAC-2 interceptors, which are primarily used against aircraft and cruise missiles, continue to be delivered under the PURL program.
A well-informed source at NATO noted that the issue of the PAC-3 missile delay is currently being discussed at a high political level.
However, officials currently do not know when exactly this situation with the delivery delays will improve.
Earlier, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky stated that the U.S. is delaying the delivery of interceptor missiles that have already been fully paid for by European allies.
According to him, part of these deliveries under the PURL program is still awaiting final approval from Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth.
At the same time, over the past 90 days, the United States has transferred only 24 anti-aircraft missiles for the Patriot systems to the Ukrainian side.
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio explained the delay by the need to balance commitments to partners with the U.S.’s own needs for protecting its facilities.
At the same time, the head of the U.S. State Department assured that there was no deliberate political directive from Washington to harm Ukraine.
According to data from analysts at the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) for July 2026, U.S. PAC-3 stockpiles have decreased from over 2,300 to fewer than 830 units.

articles.title: Seven oil tankers carrying 288,000 tonnes of Russian diesel sail towards US
articles.body:
Seven oil tankers carrying an estimated 288,000 tonnes of Russian diesel are now sailing towards the US, though it is uncertain if the vessels will be able to unload amid a political row about the legality of the shipments.
The transport, tracked by the pressure group Greenpeace, is the first phase of a contentious supply deal negotiated between presidents Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin earlier this month, reversing years of sanctions on Russia oil.
Previous reports had counted three tankers that had departed Russian oil terminals in the Baltic Sea, but using a range of sources, including shipping tracking websites, Greenpeace believes its monitoring exercise is the most complete yet.
Shaun Burnie, an energy specialist with Greenpeace Ukraine, argued that now the location of the tankers could be plotted on a map, the shipments should be halted by Congress or local authorities in the US.
“Instead of rewarding Russia for its vile war against Ukraine, there needs to be more punitive sanctions against Russia,” he said. “These shipments can be stopped”.
One of the seven tankers, Taurus, is relatively close to the US, but at the time the map was first published, five of the others were close to the UK, and three were sailing through or into the English Channel.
In Ukraine, 14 people were reported killed on Thursday morning when a Russian drone struck a crowded train platform in the central city of Dnipro. Five others were reported killed in daytime strikes in two other cities, Chernihiv and Kremenchuk.
Ukrzaliznytsia, Ukraine’s state railway company, said a high speed jet-powered drone had struck as a commuter train was preparing to depart Dnipro’s main station. Bodies lay scattered after the relatively unusual daytime attack, which took place at around 11am.
Putin agreed to supply the US with 1.8m tonnes of diesel in a surprise deal announced on 9 October, starting with 300,000 tonnes immediately. Trump announced a six-month waiver on existing sanctions to allow the shipments to proceed.
Russia had been hit by waves of economic sanctions from the US, EU, UK and other leading western economies since Putin launched the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. But this autumn, Trump has altered course and tried to work more closely with Putin, even though Russia has not stopped attacking its neighbour.
Earlier this week, a group of US lawmakers, led by a handful of Democratic senators, warned banks and port authorities that they could face congressional investigations and other legal action if they handled the Russian diesel.
Mikie Sherrill, the Democratic governor of New Jersey, said she was looking at how to prevent the diesel from being unloaded, if an attempt was made to do so in her state. She described the deal as “corrupt and illegal”.
There have been reports that the White House has been trying to encourage US firms to take the oil, though it is not clear buyers are forthcoming, given the legal risks so close to next Tuesday’s midterm elections.
Trump’s popularity has waned as fuel prices in the US have soared since he attacked Iran in the spring. Polling suggests a high likelihood that control of the House of Representatives could pass to the Democrats in the elections, while the battle over the Senate is considered too close to call.
The US president had argued that the Russia deal would help lower diesel prices, though the price per gallon has risen from $6.28 at the time the agreement was announced to $6.33, according to the American Automobile Association.
Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, denounced the agreement because the money raised would help the Kremlin fund the ongoing war. “Backroom deals” gave Putin more chances on the battlefield, he said.
The Kremlin has been trying to keep information about the latest oil exports secret. A presidential decree from the end of September restricted the publication of information about oil exports in an effort to evade international sanctions.

Zelenskyy's commissioner: Russian missiles contain many US components
Russia continues to use American microchips in the production of ballistic and cruise missiles, as it has not yet managed to replace them with Russian components.

articles.title: Putin explains why he welcomed rare call from Nordic leaders
articles.body:
Putin explains why he welcomed rare call from Nordic leaders
Russian President Vladimir Putin has welcomed a rare phone call from the leaders of Finland and Norway, saying Moscow has always supported efforts to normalize relations with European countries.
Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store spoke with Putin on Tuesday, breaking with the longstanding practice among Western European leaders of avoiding direct contact with Moscow since the escalation of the Ukraine conflict in February 2022. The initiative drew criticism from Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen, who questioned its effectiveness and said it had not been coordinated with European partners.
Speaking at a press conference in the Kremlin on Thursday, Putin said he welcomed dialogue with Western countries despite their military support for Ukraine and sanctions against Russia.
“I believe it was the right thing to do. After all, there are people in Europe who, unlike some others, do not want to inflict a ‘strategic defeat’ on Russia but instead want to establish some kind of constructive dialogue,” Putin said.
He added that Russia would support “any steps aimed at restoring full-fledged and comprehensive relations” with European countries, whether through the EU as a whole or on a bilateral basis.
Putin reiterated that Russia was not seeking a broader conflict with the EU or NATO. “We do not want any war with Europe. If some of them want one, let them prepare. But they have not achieved their goal of inflicting a ‘strategic defeat’ on Russia, and it is unlikely that this will be possible by 2030,” he said.
And if things go too far, there will be no winners at all. Let no one forget that.
The leaders of Norway and Finland said they had sought to convey messages directly to Putin “regarding future negotiations to help to end the war,” ahead of US-mediated Russia-Ukraine talks expected to take place in Abu Dhabi in the near future. They described the conversation as a follow-up to their meeting with Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky in Oslo on October 20.
Norway and the Kremlin disputed a report by the British newspaper Financial Times claiming that Putin had spent much of the call lecturing his counterparts on Russian and Slavic history.
Stubb has cultivated a close relationship with US President Donald Trump, with whom he has frequently discussed the Ukraine conflict, earning him the nickname “Trump whisperer” in Western media.
The Finnish leader has also emphasized his country’s long experience of dealing with Russia. Finland shares a 1,340-kilometer border with its eastern neighbor and maintained peaceful, if sometimes uneasy, relations with Moscow throughout the Cold War.
The call came amid growing tensions between Kiev and Washington after Trump lifted sanctions on Russian diesel exports and subsequently waived additional restrictions following Zelensky’s refusal to halt strikes on Russian oil refineries, which Trump blamed for soaring fuel prices.
Moscow has repeatedly accused European leaders of sabotaging the 2022 peace talks with Ukraine and seeking to undermine Trump’s ongoing efforts to broker a deal.

articles.title: Chinese warships and aircraft operate around Taiwan overnight
articles.body:
- Taiwan detected six Chinese military aircraft, seven navy ships and one official ship around the island in the 24 hours to Oct. 29.
- Five aircraft entered Taiwan’s air defense identification zone, and four fighter and drone sorties crossed the Taiwan Strait median line.
Taiwan detected six Chinese military aircraft, seven People’s Liberation Army Navy ships and one Chinese official ship operating around the island in the 24 hours to 6 a.m. local time on Oct. 29, the Ministry of National Defense said on social media.
Five of the six aircraft sorties entered the northern, central and southwestern parts of Taiwan’s air defense identification zone, or ADIZ, a buffer area where Taipei asks approaching aircraft to identify themselves. The zone extends well beyond the island’s territorial airspace, and flights into it are not violations of Taiwanese airspace. The ministry said its forces monitored the activity and responded with combat air patrol aircraft, navy ships and coastal missile systems.
A map released with the report shows two separate groups of flights. Between 9:35 a.m. and 5:20 p.m. on Oct. 28, five sorties of fighters and drones operated along the median line of the Taiwan Strait, the informal boundary between the two sides, and four of them crossed it. A single fighter flew near the northern edge of the zone, north of Taiwan, between 1:55 p.m. and 2 p.m.
The ministry did not identify the aircraft or drone types, the classes of the seven navy ships, or what kind of government vessel the official ship was.
Chinese military aircraft and ships operate around Taiwan almost daily, and Taipei publishes a tally each morning. The figures vary widely from day to day. On busier days the ministry has reported dozens of aircraft, including one 24-hour period when 38 sorties and nine navy ships were detected and 31 aircraft crossed the median line. During large-scale exercises announced by China’s Eastern Theater Command, Taiwan has reported dozens of aircraft and vessels in a single day and put its forces on high alert.
The median line has no legal standing, but for decades both sides treated it as an unofficial dividing line that helped keep military aircraft apart in the narrow strait. Chinese aircraft now cross it routinely, and Taiwan’s ministry tracks each crossing in its daily reports.

articles.title: Pentagon fires general it says leaked classified information to media
articles.body:
Pentagon fires general it says leaked classified information to media
Army Lieutenant General Brett Sylvia was subject of investigation into leaking information about Iran and Ukraine.
United States Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has fired the director of the Strategy, Plans and Policy Directorate at the Joint Chiefs of Staff, Lieutenant General Brett Sylvia, for what the Pentagon says is severe misconduct. The move comes amid reports that the US had warned its allies of a possible renewal of strikes against Iran.
A Department of Defense official told Al Jazeera on Thursday that Sylvia had been “meeting with journalists outside the Pentagon in order to leak classified information”.
“Sylvia is the subject of an investigation for leaking classified information about the Iran war, the war between Russia and Ukraine, and more,” the official added.
The investigation into Sylvia remains ongoing and has been referred to the Department of Justice for further action, according to the Pentagon.
The official said Sylvia was the Defense Department’s chief military planner but “was not a central planner for the Iran war”. “That is the responsibility of CENTCOM [Central Command] and its commander, Admiral [Brad] Cooper,” the official said.
Sylvia’s firing comes as Trump has repeatedly floated starting new military operations against Iran.
He is the second person to be ousted from the post, known in military circles as the J5, under Hegseth. His predecessor was forced to retire in October last year.
“Sylvia failed three polygraphs which questioned him about leaking classified information,” the Pentagon official said while accusing Sylvia of putting national security at risk.
“Urgent action was needed and could not wait another second,” he concluded.
There is no immediate replacement for Sylvia, according to an official who spoke on the condition of anonymity to The Associated Press news agency.
Before arriving at the Joint Chiefs of Staff, Sylvia served as commander of the 101st Airborne Division at Fort Campbell, Kentucky, until May 2025, according to his official biography, which has now been taken offline. He also previously served as the vice director for the office he recently led.
His military awards include six Bronze Star Medals, including one for valour, and a Purple Heart, indicating he was wounded in combat.
Sean Parnel, assistant to the defense secretary for public affairs, said earlier on Thursday in a post on X that “the Department of War has zero tolerance for the intentional, unauthorized disclosure of classified information.” He did not refer specifically to Sylvia.
Sylvia is the latest senior Pentagon official whom Hegseth has accused of leaking to the media. He fired three aides from his inner circle last year as part of a broader leak investigation that included polygraph tests.
President Donald Trump has promised to “finish the job” in Iran after launching the war with Israel eight months ago and said he would do so after the midterm elections on Tuesday.

articles.title: Ten US military aircraft arrive in Israel as Americans warn of 'short, focused' Iran war - report
articles.body:
Ten US Air Force (USAF) transport aircraft arrived at IAF bases in southern Israel as part of a larger Middle East air convoy transferring military equipment across the region, KAN News reported on Thursday.
The aircraft, which came from Texas' Fort Bliss base, are likely stocked with air defense systems intended to protect regional assets amid reported US warnings earlier this week of a potential "short, focused war with Iran," according to KAN.
Fort Bliss base hosts one of the US military's largest air defense stockpiles, with the report suggesting that the aircraft may be replenishing US interceptor missiles in Israel on systems like THAAD and Patriot.
Other aircraft in the air convoy landed in Jordan, Qatar, and Saudi Arabia, with the KAN report coming after an earlier report that the US had transferred an additional Patriot system to the region pending a potential escalation with Iran.
The report did not specify which transport aircraft arrived in Israel, though they are likely C-5M Super Galaxys, C-17 Globemaster IIIs, or a combination of the two, since both can lift such heavy cargo.
According to the report, the aircraft landed at the Ovda and Nevatim IAF air bases, with Nevatim home to several F-35I squadrons.
US, Israel closely coordinating on Iran, source tells KAN
An Israeli source told KAN that the US and Israel are closely coordinating on Iran, with reports that an additional US naval aircraft carrier will join American forces in the region, alongside an additional Marine unit.

articles.title: Spain, Portugal work with Kiev to develop weapons for strikes against Russia — politician
articles.body:
MOSCOW, October 29. /TASS/. The authorities in Spain and Portugal, together with Kiev, are working to develop weapons for strikes against Russia, while their own citizens are grappling with a housing and economic crisis, Viktor Medvedchuk, head of the Other Ukraine movement and former leader of the Opposition Platform - For Life party banned in Ukraine, said.
"While the two countries on the Iberian Peninsula are trying to cope with a housing crisis and rising costs of living, their governments are engaging in increasingly extensive military cooperation with Ukraine. Behind the familiar phrase ‘support for Ukraine’ lies a far more specific reality: Spanish and Portuguese companies, together with Ukrainian manufacturers, are launching projects in the fields of missile technology, strike drones, guidance systems, and other weapons designed to strike Russia," he wrote in an article posted on the movement’s website.
According to the politician, Spain's military-industrial cooperation with Ukraine primarily concerns missile technology and long-range drones. "Portugal also emphasizes long-range drones, though in addition to aerial systems, this includes sea-based unmanned vessels," he added.
Companies cooperating with Ukrainian firms include Tekever UAS, S.A., a Portuguese drone manufacturer whose AR3 and AR5 systems have been used by the Ukrainian armed forces since 2022, as well as the Spanish companies Sener Aeroespacial, S.A. and Escribano Mechanical and Engineering, S.L.U., and others.
"As a result, the political choices made by Madrid and Lisbon seem highly contradictory. On the one hand, there is condemnation of military actions in the Persian Gulf. On the other hand, these countries are being drawn into the war in Ukraine, which requires funding and cuts to social service budgets. While Spaniards are being forced to live in tents due to the housing crisis, and Portuguese authorities acknowledge the lack of affordable housing as one of the most pressing social problems, the governments of both countries are at the same time allocating state resources, industrial capacity, and technological expertise toward expanding arms production for Ukraine," he concluded.

articles.title: How Many Su-34 Fighter-Bombers Does Russia Have Left? Ukraine’s Intelligence Has the Figures
articles.body:
- Category
- War in Ukraine
How Many Su-34 Fighter-Bombers Does Russia Have Left? Ukraine’s Intelligence Has the Figures
Russia continues to produce and modernize its Su-34 fighter-bombers despite significant losses sustained during its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, with approximately 140 aircraft of this type remaining in service as of October 22, 2026, according to Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence Directorate (HUR).
The Su-34 fighter-bomber is a key component of Russia’s strike aviation capabilities, particularly due to its use as a platform for launching guided aerial bombs against ground targets, including Ukrainian frontline positions and settlements near active combat zones.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to HUR, Russia’s Aerospace Forces currently operate approximately 140 Su-34 aircraft of various configurations, including the upgraded Su-34M, also designated Su-34NVO.
Since the beginning of the full-scale invasion, Russia has lost 43 Su-34 fighter-bombers, while another seven aircraft have sustained damage, Ukrainian intelligence reported.
These losses represent a substantial reduction in Russia’s fleet of fighter-bombers, particularly given the time, financial resources, and specialized industrial cooperation required to manufacture replacements.
HUR estimates that Russia’s current production capacity stands at approximately 14 to 18 Su-34 aircraft annually. At that rate, replacing the 43 aircraft destroyed since February 2022 would require roughly 2.5 to three years of production.
Despite these losses, Moscow continues to manufacture and upgrade the aircraft in an effort to maintain its operational fleet and sustain the intensity of missile and bomb strikes against Ukraine.
However, according to Ukrainian intelligence, Russia’s ability to expand its Su-34 fleet remains dependent on several factors, including available manufacturing capacity, access to technological components, and the defense industry’s ability to compensate for aircraft losses.
Meanwhile, Russia’s Su-34 fleet has also faced threats at the airfields where the aircraft are stationed. On October 23, Ukrainian forces carried out a missile strike against Russia’s Baltimor military airfield in Voronezh, a major base for Su-34 fighter-bombers, according to the Exilenova+ OSINT community.
Preliminary reports suggest that the attack targeted aircraft parking areas and the grounds of the former Voronezh Military Aviation Engineering University, located immediately adjacent to the airfield.

North Korea launched approximately 10 short-range ballistic missiles into waters off its east coast. Pyongyang denies involvement in the mine explosion.

Details

Kim Jong Un wants the DPRK to create the "strongest" army in the world24.10.26, 09:40 • 6054 views

articles.title: New Analysis: Air Force Should Buy 250 Blended-Wing Tankers, as 2027 Demo Looms
articles.body:
A new think tank analysis finds a hypothetical blended-wing body tanker could offer twice as much refueling performance as the KC-46A Pegasus and recommends the Air Force buy scores of them, as the service prepares to evaluate a BWB demonstrator next year and must juggle its future tanker plans with a host of other modernization priorities like fighters and bombers.
The report, released by the Hudson Institute on Oct. 27, makes the case that the Air Force needs a fleet of 250 advanced new tankers to meet the challenge of refueling operations in a potential conflict with China.
Traditionally during conflicts, the Air Force has launched tankers from uncontested airfields relatively close to bomber and fighter strike objectives. But the vast distances of the Western Pacific and the long reach of China’s missiles make that untenable, report authors Timothy A. Walton and Shane Dennin write.
By 2035, they note, Chinese forces will likely be capable of suppressing large-scale tanker operations from “the forward and many of the intermediate airfields that tankers normally rely on,” a capability that “could collapse U.S. air operations and heavily contribute to U.S. defeat in a war against the People’s Republic of China,”
The solution, they conclude, are tankers that can launch from farther afield and carry more fuel to the fight.
Blended-wing body aircraft blur the line between wings and fuselage for a design that is considered more aerodynamically efficient and has a large cabin/cargo space. The combination, the Hudson report concludes, means a “medium BWB can refuel more than twice as many force packages or refuel force packages more than twice as far as the KC-46A,” the report states. “At longer-ranges and higher offloads, the medium BWB can deliver up to five times as many operationally relevant increments of fuel as the KC-46A.”
Since 2023, the Air Force has been developing a BWB demonstrator/prototype program with startup JetZero, which is partnering with Northrop Grumman. That aircraft, dubbed Z4, is expected to make its first flight in 2027.
An Air Force spokesperson confirmed that the “blended-wing body project is currently active, on schedule, and meeting assembly milestones; the demonstrator’s first flight is scheduled for late 2027.”
JetZero has proposed a tanker variant, dubbed KC-Z4, though the demonstrator will not be a refueler.
The Air Force’s future tanker plans are not settled—the Eisenhower-era KC-135 fleet is showing its age, and officials have stressed the need for refuelers that can survive in contested airspace. At one point, they were exploring concepts through the Next-Generation Aerial Refueling System program, but they shifted gears in the 2027 budget request, saying they would focus on protection systems over a new aircraft.
Meanwhile, the service is still planning on buying up to 75 additional KC-46 Pegasus refuelers on top of the current program of record for 188. In May, the Air Force signed an agreement with Boeing to fix critical issues with the Pegasus, such as fielding an improved remote vision system that boom operators use to refuel other aircraft—a requirement that senior leaders have said must be resolved before the Air Force will sign the new contract extension to buy an extra 75 tankers.
The Hudson paper recommends the Air Force move forward with the KC-46 production extension contract. Then, assuming the BWB demonstrator evaluation goes well in 2027 and 2028, the service should direct fiscal 2027 research, development, test and evaluation funding to “mature medium-sized, long-range, high-offload capacity tanker designs, such as medium BWB,” the report states.
“Our proposed plan’s yearly tanker costs would require additional RDTE outlays in the late 2020s and early 2030s, but its total RDTE, procurement, and operations and support costs over 30 years could amount to $15.5 billion less than a plan that solely procured KC-46A,” according to the report, which compared acquiring and operating 250 Medium BWB tankers to the same number of KC-46s.
Retired Air Force Gen. Mike Minihan, who led Air Mobility Command between 2021 and 2024, said he saw the potential of the BWB demonstrator effort when it was conceived as a way to reverse the service’s neglect of tanker fleet modernization when compared to efforts to develop fifth- and sixth-generation bombers and fighters.
“One of my biggest concerns was the equilibrium of the strike force with the enabling force; I love B-21, I love F-15 EX, I love F-35, I love the [Collaborative Combat Aircraft], … but if we don’t invest in the enablers to make those things successful, we’re going to look silly on the modern battlefield,” said Minihan, who retired in 2024.
Minihan said his continued belief in the BWB design convinced him to become an advisor to JetZero earlier this year.
“It’s almost two times everything—two times fuel the efficiency, two times the amount of receiver service, two times quicker, two times the distance—I mean, it’s quite remarkable,” he said.
Douglas Birkey, Executive Director for AFA’s Mitchell Institute for Aerospace Studies, also noted the potential benefits of the BWB design.
“There is no question the Air Force needs new refueling capacity, and it needs to ensure that it can maximize offload range—you want to haul as much fuel as possible, not burn a whole lot on your way to the refueling track, offload as much as possible and then get back home,” Birkey said. “And the blended-wing body has definite, distinct aerodynamic advantages, being highly efficient to maximize that off-loader range.”
But Birkey said he is skeptical whether the Air Force can commit to a long-term funding plan for a next-generation BWB tanker in the current budget environment. The service’s $267.7 billion budget request in fiscal 2027 is $53 billion more than it 2026 budget, but even then, competing modernization priorities such as the sixth-generation B-21 bomber and F-47 fighter limited any investment in tanker fleet modernization. Buying a new fleet of BWB tankers would require even larger toplines of reliable funding over the next decade for the service.
“There’s got to be sustained long-term investment; this isn’t a one-year plus-up kind of investment. They need a decade’s worth of solid investment,” Birkey said. “They’re making up for so much underinvestment.”
For its report, Hudson evaluated the KC-46A, the Airbus A330 MRTT+, a medium-sized BWB design, a medium-sized reduced signature design, and a collaborative tanker aircraft—the latter two to theoretically shuttle tank from parent tankers such as the KC-46A at short-to-moderate distances. The KC-46A and A330 MRTT+ are medium-range, multirole designs while the Medium BWB is a long-range, high offload dedicated tanker. The medium BWB tanker is being designed to carry 300,000 pounds of fuel compared to the KC-46’s max capacity of 212,000 pounds of fuel. The A330 MRTT+ can carry 245,000 pounds of fuel.
Hudson concluded that the Air Force should take a holistic approach that includes:
- Prioritizing military construction and other funding to enhance capacity and resilience of its most important tanker airfields.
- Continuing to increase funding for command, control, and communications; self-defense; fuel transfer; and automation and autonomy mission systems for current and future tankers.
- Developing and procuring 250 medium-sized, long-range, high-offload tankers, such as the medium BWB, which could prove capable of standing in a moderate distance from threats.
The Air Force could begin fielding the new fleet of medium BWBs by the mid-2030s “for reasonable RDTE and procurement costs that align with projected budgets, and it could cost considerably less than simply buying more KC-46As,” the report states.
The report estimates that a mixed fleet with roughly 260 KC-46s and 250 medium BWB tankers would run $398 billion in totals costs over 30 years, while fielding an additional 250 KC-46s for a total fleet of 510 would cost $413 billion.
Both aircraft in the mixed fleet would complement each other, the report states: “Together, the force could succeed in its most stressing scenarios, as well as sustainably execute other operations across the world.”
Minihan said he agrees that the Air Force needs “bombers and fighters of fifth and sixth generation, but we generally don’t pay attention to the enabling force until it fails. … To think that we can take a four-generation gap between our strike force and our enabling force into combat with a near-peer adversary is a fool’s errand.”
Minihan said he was “on the record from my time in uniform as supporting” the medium BWB demonstrator effort. “It fits perfectly into the NGAS concept,” Minihan said. “Every pound of gas I save getting to the fight is a pound of gas I can give away to a fighter or a bomber.”

articles.title: “The enemy has changed tactics”: Zaporizhzhia faces record number of Russian FPV drone attacks, hitting public transport 3 times in one day
articles.body:
Zaporizhzhia experienced a record number of Russian FPV drone attacks on 29 October, injuring 14 people, including a 14-year-old boy, regional authorities said.
Russian forces used FPV drones and multiple-launch rocket systems to attack civilian infrastructure, targeting municipal transport and damaging residential buildings, warehouses, and cars, prosecutors said.
Zaporizhzhia reports record FPV drone attacks
Zaporizhzhia Regional Military Administration head Mykhailo Semikin said Zaporizhzhia had experienced a record number of FPV drone attacks on Thursday. After meeting with military officials, he said the authorities were aware of the situation and relevant services and Ukrainian defenders were responding.
He said Russian forces had “changed their tactics and modified their drones,” adding that Ukrainian military personnel were working on countermeasures to address the new threats.
Semikin urged residents to remain calm, heed air raid alerts, and exercise particular caution.
Russian drones target municipal transport
The attacks included strikes on a municipal bus, a minibus, and a trolleybus, according to Semikin.
In the morning, a Russian FPV drone struck a municipal bus, injuring four people.
In a separate attack, Russian forces struck 15 vehicles, a warehouse building, and a power line, sparking a fire and damaging a nearby apartment building. Two men, aged 41 and 66, were injured.
At around midday, another FPV drone hit a minibus in central Zaporizhzhia, injuring one person.
Later, a Russian drone struck a municipal trolleybus, critically injuring a 56-year-old woman and lightly injuring two other women, aged 71 and 66.
Zaporizhzhia’s proximity to the front line
Zaporizhzhia lies relatively close to the front line in southern Ukraine, leaving the city exposed to Russian attacks with weapons that can be used at shorter ranges, including FPV drones and multiple-launch rocket systems.
The proximity allows Russian forces to threaten civilian infrastructure more easily without relying solely on long-range missiles or drones.
Prosecutors investigate suspected war crime
The Zaporizhzhia Regional Prosecutor’s Office said it had opened a war crimes investigation. Investigators from the Security Service of Ukraine’s regional directorate are conducting the pretrial investigation.
The casualty count and damage reports were preliminary, and authorities said information was still being updated as the attacks continued.
Russian attacks kill civilians in several Ukrainian cities
Zaporizhzhia was not the only major city hit by Russian attacks on 29 October. In Dnipro, a Russian strike on the railway station killed at least 14 people.
In Chernihiv, two teenage girls were killed and 23 people injured, including four children. In Kremenchuk, Poltava Oblast, three people were killed and 15 injured, including three children.
The attacks damaged residential buildings and civilian infrastructure in all three cities.

articles.title: ‘If this works, it will be the first real ceasefire across a large stretch of the front’: Russia and Ukraine maintain truce in occupied Oleshky for more than two days
articles.body:
‘If this works, it will be the first real ceasefire across a large stretch of the front’: Russia and Ukraine maintain truce in occupied Oleshky for more than two days
Russia and Ukraine have halted hostilities around the occupied city of Oleshky since October 27. The Verkhovna Rada’s human rights commissioner, Dmytro Lubinets, confirmed on the morning of October 29 that the ceasefire had held for more than two days. Russia’s human rights commissioner, Yana Lantratova, said humanitarian aid — “food, fuel, medicine, and hygiene products” — had been sent to Oleshky.
Lubinets and Lantratova set out for Oleshky on the afternoon of October 29. Lubinets will be the first Ukrainian official of such rank to visit Russian-occupied territories. Both commissioners said their main task is to deliver humanitarian aid to residents and ensure the safe evacuation of those who want to leave.
Sources who spoke to the Ukrainian news outlet Ukrainska Pravda and were involved in organizing the ceasefire said the ceasefire around Oleshky is meant to test whether Ukrainian and Russian military commanders can carry out political agreements to end hostilities.
Organizing a halt to the fighting turned out to be “an extremely difficult task,” according to the outlet’s sources. A political order to cease fire does not by itself guarantee automatic compliance on the front line, a source in Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky’s administration told Ukrainska Pravda. Even Ukrainian troops demanded guarantees several times that if they stopped, “nothing bad would happen afterward,” the source said. The source explained:
We want to get the military — both our General Staff and the Russian one — used to the idea that if the political leadership has decided that in a given sector of the front we stop, freeze in place, and no one opens fire, the military can make that happen. They can guarantee it. Not a situation where the political leadership has reached an agreement and the military says, “Sorry, we can’t stop, we’ve got something going on.”
It is easier for the Russian side than for the Ukrainian side to organize and maintain a ceasefire, according to Ukrainska Pravda’s sources. “They [the Russians] have a rigid military vertical. We have a decentralized army. And someone — some well-known military blogger — could stir up the mood on air so much that everything falls apart afterward,” a source said.
If the ceasefire in Oleshky can be maintained, as planned, until the evening of November 1, the Ukrainian side expects to repeat this kind of local ceasefire later along other parts of the front. “That’s precisely so the military can learn how to do this: stop, ensure safe passage, and so on. So that later, if there’s some major agreement, we could implement it right away,” a source who spoke to Ukrainska Pravda said.
If this works, this will be the first example of a real ceasefire across a fairly large stretch of the front. It’s come at such a cost — the military, Russia’s Federal Security Service, and everyone else are doing nothing but trying to sabotage it. But we believe it will work out and that this will set a precedent.
The war in photographs
Russia’s Defense Ministry announced that it had begun clearing mines from roads leading into Oleshky and published photos and video of sappers at work. Russian President Vladimir Putin, speaking at a plenary session of the Russia–Africa summit underway in Moscow, claimed it was Ukraine that had mined the approaches to Oleshky, creating “practically a humanitarian catastrophe.”
